This study examines the discretization of an optimal stochastic control problem involving the parabolic differential equations, with both control variables included in diffusion. Through this study, convergence for this problem is established, even in situations where the input data involves unbounded values. The part of the proof that ensures this result involves deriving estimates of the second order for time and first order for space discretization errors.

This study analyzes the highest-energy cosmic rays accessible via the Pierre Auger Observatory, specifically within the 56–97 EeV energy range (1 EeV equals $10^{18}$ eV). By examining events of the same type from both hemispheres of the celestial sphere, the research identifies a clear anisotropy directed toward the galactic plane for energies exceeding 8 EeV. This finding indicates that the observed directional asymmetry is not merely a reflection of primary cosmic ray directions but likely results from significant secondary interactions within the detector. Furthermore, the analysis determines that the energy function describing the increasing angular size of Galactic-originating cosmic rays remains consistent with previous high-energy measurements up to approximately 1 EeV times 100, a result that supports current top-down models.

This work presents the proof that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra defined over any field exhibits a null structure. This finding goes beyond an earlier outcome by others, which only demonstrated these algebras to be solvable.

This study presents the initial experimental results regarding fluctuations in the transverse momentum component along the beam direction ($p_{T\,beam}$) for $U+U$ systems at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 193 GeV, based on a dataset of 1.54 million events collected by the LHC Energy Positron Collider (LHC). Flutation observations were quantified using the relative standard deviation ($\sigma/\langle x\rangle$) across various $p_{T\,beam}$ intervals, covering from 0.2 to 2.0 TeV per particle. This study examines the challenges and complications involved in representing knowledge table inconsistencies alongside their related measures of data quality. By presenting a framework that addresses these table-level discrepancies and reliability metrics, we demonstrate how this information can be effectively integrated into various graphical user interface (GUI) elements of knowledge table applications. Focusing on Microsoft's Socratic Tables as a case study, we highlight existing limitations in displaying such inconsistencies and propose concrete enhancements. Additionally, to support further research, we make the associated prototype software and measures available to the public through this project.

This article introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, designed specifically for analyzing and forecasting count time series data. {W}e establish the theory underlying the quasi-maximum likelihood (QMLE) estimator for the TV-PARA model and demonstrate that this estimator is consistent and converges at an appropriate rate. Furthermore, we show that since parameter estimates vary across different time instances, the resulting parameter uncertainty induces variability in forecast outcomes; consequently, prediction intervals are established to reflect this specific type of uncertainty. To address both forecasting and estimation, we propose a linear combination of historical observations and exogenous variables as the method to update time-varying coefficients adaptively. The efficacy of the suggested approach is validated through simulated examples and real-world applications involving actual count series, with results indicating that the TV-PARA model outperforms standard linear alternatives in accuracy.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation designed to address robotic object manipulation by enforcing SE(3)-equivariance to ensure reliable view-generalizing pick-and-place operations. To achieve view-generalization, our approach incorporates a periodic 1D convolutional network that maps the Neural Volume Field into object-part descriptors. Furthermore, we define a Neural Hand to handle contact dynamics, utilizing an inverse kinematics network to convert a desired object pose into specific hand pose configurations required for grasping and placement tasks. We validate our approach through experiments utilizing a learned contact model to evaluate various grasp and placement behaviors across multiple tasks, highlighting the significance of contact modeling in automated manipulation. Additionally, to demonstrate the theoretical SE(3)-equivariance of our framework, we provide a mathematical proof specific to the developed Neural Hand.

By implementing the functional renormalization group method at next-to-leading order within the derivative expansion, we enhance previous predictions regarding the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity across standard O(N) universality classes. Our analysis indicates that for N=2—corresponding to the 3-state Potts model—the ratio |z_c|/R_chi^{1/gamma} achieves a value of 1.495 +/- 0.010. This result implies the Raynaud conjecture is likely correct.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to solve generic graphical lasso problems. This scheme enables the estimation of the inverse covariance matrix for high-dimensional data using various penalty functions and prior constraints. Users can define custom penalties and restrictions, making it suitable for implementing specialized approaches like graphically correlated lasso methods. To facilitate analysis, GGLasso offers various statistical visualization tools specifically for the examination of precision matrices within the resulting models.

This study examines and compares numerous numerical techniques designed to solve the configurational averaging problem arising in Biомolecule modeling via Molecular Dynamics (specifically, Brownian Dynamics). The work offers a thorough review and formulation of these approaches. The comparison focuses on attributes such as particle strength, theoretical biases, and the practical implementation details. The authors argue that enhancing the accuracy of configurational averaging through advanced algorithms—without increasing supercomputing resources—is a key avenue for improving Brownian Dynamics applications. The study provides derived expression for particle strengths and discusses the practical and theoretical merits of various strategies, including stochastic and deterministic integrators applied to both white and colored noise scenarios. A distinct advantage of these new algorithms over earlier methods is their ability to utilize larger time steps while maintaining second-order particle strength. The text concludes by outlining potential future extensions, such as implementing these schemes in three dimensions to handle many-body hydrodynamic interactions through convergent series based on reflection principles.

We introduce a novel method for computing a specific type of eigenvector centrality applicable to multilayer networks subject to cross-layer constraints on node significance. These networks consist of multiple layers, where each provides a distinct connection type between nodes; since layers represent different interaction modes, a node's influence within one can affect its significance in another. Furthermore, our framework accounts for various multilayer scenarios defined by how significance constraints operate. To calculate this centrality measures, we formulate an optimization problem solved via an alternating algorithm that initially assumes significance uniformly distributed across all layers and subsequently adjusts it. We validate our framework using synthetic data and apply it to a real-world air transport multilayer network to de-risk political vulnerabilities in de-risking key nodes within an air transport system.

A persistent conjecture posits that global symmetries cannot exist within quantum gravity. We challenge this by presenting a scenario of generalized $\theta$-terms that act as absolute, classical, global symmetries which remain protected against all corrections, including those from gravity. Because these terms are linear in curvature, they are unrenormalizable and susceptible to gravitational corrections; consequently, the extreme precision with which their coefficients must be initialized effectively constitutes an impracticably high-order condition, rendering it indistinguishable from an exact symmetry. We further speculate that the only global symmetries permitted in gravity are those tied to massless degrees of freedom with non-negative dimensions, meaning their coupling constants are marginal or irrelevant, and thus their initial values require equally precise setups. Since generalized $\theta$-terms fit this category, their symmetry is effectively exact from a coarse-graining perspective, satisfying the massless pole criterion.

Through {\it ab initio} band structure calculations, we identify that the natural sulfide copper source, cubanite ($\text{CuFe}_2\text{S}_4$ in the antiferrite structure), presents an unexpected case where all $3d$ copper orbitals participate equally in chemical bonding. This finding contrasts with similar compounds like $\text{CuGaS}_2$ and chalcogenides containing group 4 cations, which typically display highly orbital-selective characteristics, often restricting bonding to just $d_{xy}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals. Furthermore, the electronic arrangement in cubanite allows for a direct comparison with the well-studied mineral $\text{CuAl}_2\text{O}_4$, substituting the spin-spin interaction between copper and aluminum with copper and iron. Despite this sp-spin similarity, swapping the spin for a sp interaction transforms sp$^{\dagger}$-mediated interactions into sp$^{\dagger}$-type interactions, which in turn modifies spin-orbit coupling effects. Such spin-spin differences have significant implications regarding spin-spin magnetic ordering. The calculated band structures and related properties offer a detailed framework to understand cubanite's nature and account for the absence of observed spin order in related spin-spin models.

Using a MoSe2/CdS type-II heterostructure, we demonstrate the generation and manipulation of a quantum dot containing an excitation lifetime exceeding 1 nanosecond, with radiative efficiency approaching 100%. These findings indicate that quantum dots within type-II heterostructures offer advantages over bright excitons in monolayer and type-I quantum wells from both a fundamental perspective and practical applications, particularly by enabling significantly longer coherence times and significantly extended spin storage times due to the use of dark excitons.

In this work, we investigate the characterization of Single-Photon Catalyzed Coherent States (SPCCSs), a class of nonclassical states defined by a process where a coherent state undergoes interaction with a single photon followed by the trivial trace-out (or "catalysis") of that photon. Our analysis examines their statistical features, including the calculation of photon number distributions, the evaluation of various nonclassicality indicators, and the analysis of thermal and intensity fluctuations. Additionally, we determine the optimal superposition of an SPCCS state and its complex conjugate required to achieve anti-bunching behavior. These findings offer theoretical insights into the fundamental attributes of SPCCSs and provide practical guidelines for utilizing these states in quantum optical applications.

The application of bivectors within General Relativity and the Newman-Penrose formalism is explored. In this context, bivectors function as elements of the algebra associated with a given reference frame. Our approach begins by formulating the associated star-algebra in an frame-independent manner and subsequently expresses all NP quantities and equations using this algebra. The resulting framework yields a conceptual interpretation of the NP formalism that is both novel and coherent. The use of bivectors facilitates the derivation of several significant identities, including the Froodike relations, while also clarifying the structural logic behind the entire Newman-Penrose system. The article concludes by offering an n-bitter generalization of the NF formalism.

Within this paper, we present a new design strategy for compounds by offering efficient design algorithms that operate on molecular graphs. We also present the implementation of our proposed method using the OpenNLP framework, demonstrating its effectiveness through various molecular datasets."

Delineating esophageal tumors in CT scans presents a dual challenge for both manual and automatic segmentation: visually, these lesions often blend indistinguishably with surrounding healthy tissue, while structurally, their shapes fluctuate significantly due to the organ's complex anatomy and the imaging process itself. To mitigate the time consumption and high costs associated with annotation for self-segmentation methods, this study introduces a robust framework for esophageal tumor segmentation in CT data. The proposed algorithm begins by generating an initial marking through convolution of the image with an active contour prior (ACP) model trained on a dataset of 300 convex templates. Subsequently, the active contour evolves to produce a precise final delineation guided by image gradients and the initial convolutional label, integrating both shape and area constraints into an energy minimization framework. Evaluation against annotations from 109 cases revealed that the accurate application of area constraints was critical, with the method's efficacy heavily dependent on the density of ACP training labels. Tests on an additional set of unannotated data using shape and area dual constraints yielded an average Intersection over Union (IoU) score of 0.661. Comparative analysis indicates that this approach outperforms both active contour with edge detection and active shape models, while also surpassing automatic techniques including those based solely on convolutional neural networks (CNN).

Defined as advanced capability in two or more languages for both spoken and written communication, multilingualism frequently manifests through code-switching or code-mixing within individual sentences. This work reviews existing natural language processing (NLP) literature regarding its limitations and obstacles when addressing five critical social impact areas: crisis response, healthcare support, political engagement, anti-disinformation initiatives, and hate speech mitigation in multilingual communities. Furthermore, we introduce prospective solutions, datasets, and resources tailored to build robust multilingual models that integrate the benefits of switching. Our outlook aims to motivate the research community to prioritize the sociolinguistic realities of multilingualism in future developments, thereby fostering impactful applications across diverse global domains.

Automatic image description models are typically built, evaluated, and compared using the Microsoft Azure Cognitive Services Image Caption API evaluation framework. This paper proposes an alternative evaluation method that leverages the same data sources as the Azure image pairs to create a completely independent test set. To better reflect real-world conditions, we argue that a strict "independence" between pairs is more critical than it is for other visual tasks like image classification or retrieval. Consequently, this work defines pairs independence with a new intersection-based metric for it and provides analysis demonstrating how different document selection strategies impact this new independence metric. Additionally, we analyze the distribution of training documents based on image class similarity to support our definition of pair strict independence. Finally, utilizing this new independence metric as a foundation, we evaluate the performance of the Microsoft Azure caption generation model against two other state-of-the-art natural image description systems from Google and Facebook.

To model spatial proton therapy accurately, this research examined the scattering of 150 MeV/proton uranium ions onto multiple Ta$_2$O$_5$ samples with varying thicknesses and structural qualities. The study measured the energy and velocity spectra of produced fragments using PIPS detectors and a silicon strip telescope, respectively, while also recorded proton residual energy distributions through the Delta-E/Rad-Wilson score method to map Rp and energy spreading in oxide targets. Previous studies have shown that the presence of misinformation and its spread are influenced by individual traits, with research on conscientiousness specifically demonstrating that lower levels correlate with both the creation and sharing of such content. This paper utilizes U.S. Census data to measure state-level conscientiousness and examines its relationship with news-related metrics, including the circulation of misleading information, as indicated by Poynter's "Fake News Map," the volume of social media news interactions, Twitter activity related to top stories, and news sharing statistics from Facebook. The empirical analysis reveals a significant negative correlation between conscientiousness at the state level and each of these news dissemination indicators. The authors argue that this relationship likely stems from individual traits scaling up across geographic levels and does not necessarily imply that entire states share these characteristics. Furthermore, robustness checks confirm that the findings hold even after accounting for other major demographic variables, suggesting that the impact of unconscientiousness on news sharing remains significant after controlling for them in multivariate models. In summary, the study finds that unconscientiousness drives the dissemination of misinformation and its associated engagement, a pattern that operates through the aggregation of individual behaviors rather than collective state attributes.

Human teachers typically select specific objects, environments, and timing when demonstrating new tasks, raising the inquiry as to whether these choices impact task execution for robots. This study introduces a five-arm task learning system designed to investigate how varying object selections, settings, and temporal alignments during demonstrations influence a robot's ability to learn tasks via audio instructions. We evaluate this system using both human teachers and a robotic assistant to perform audio-based water-filling demonstrations and reproductions using Indriya. Results from automated and robotic evaluations compare audio generated by collaborative teachers against that generated individually, comparing easy and difficult cooperative scenarios against one another, and comparing all against the more straightforward case of collaborative object choices made to facilitate successful task execution using Indriya using simulated cooperation and real cooperation. The five arm system advances automated collaboration in audio-based task learning systems, enhancing the robustness of independent verification systems.

Defining quantum field theory complexity is challenging due to the infinite degrees of freedom in such systems. This review focuses on measuring complexity for conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, highlighting insights gained regarding the distinction between complex physical states and simple states, as well on the difference simple and complex operators. Additionally, I outline several unresolved challenges within the study of computational complexity within the quantum mechanical context.

Conversational interfaces, utilizing natural language interfaces and voice, enable users to interact with digital services through human-like conversations. Research in this field focuses on two key areas: (i) analyzing user queries to support, enhance, or develop natural language applications, and (ii) developing robust systems to handle these queries effectively. This thesis examines these topics through three distinct research contributions. The first investigates the evolution of user intent within a specific context—the "Music" application developed by Google Assistant—using data from Google Analytics. By applying Automatic Data Coding (ADC) techniques, the study found that music-related queries evolve significantly over time due to changes in user behavior and the application's features, with these trends holding true regardless of whether the analysis context was considered. Additionally, an analysis of support versus enhancement actions revealed that while both increase over time, support actions decline more rapidly, suggesting that evolving features primarily drive query diversity. Furthermore, an examination of temporal variations in support and enhancement actions revealed that support actions follow a weekly cycle, whereas feature-driven changes follow a monthly pattern. In addition, analyzing support actions revealed that the "Google Assistant" component accounts for over 90\% of such interventions, indicating that user feedback is predominantly directed toward improving the assistant rather than other aspects of the service.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has gained significant attention for its potential to mitigate data sparsity in recommender systems, yet most existing models focus solely on enhancing user representations. They often overlook the vast information hidden within abundant item data and fail to utilize effective cross-item collaboration strategies. To address these gaps, we propose MS-Dominant Cross-domain Recommendation (MSDCR), an innovative framework designed to simultaneously sparse-domain and multi-domain item representations. This approach leverages item information from both source and target domains to construct more robust user and cross-domain recommendations. Specifically, our sole-source item encoding module ensures accurate per-item representation using only source domain data. Furthermore, our cross-domain item encoding module enriches target domain users with similar items from the source domain, guided by a novel cross-domain attention mechanism that selectively transfers relevant item features while filtering out domain-specific noise. Our extensive experiments on three public datasets confirm that MS-Dominant significantly surpasses baseline methods in recommendation performance.

Convex optimization problems can be characterized using various representations, each yielding a distinct set of conditions that indicate exogeneity, or lack of change under transformation. When such conditions are met, these variables allow for the decentralized formulation and efficient Bag-of-Tasks execution. Exotic cones, a recent addition to the mathematical toolkit, expand the collection of problems that admit convex optimization representations by establishing correspondences between these cones and "exotic" transformations that differ from standard linear changes. In this work, we derive two such expansions utilizing the linear representation established in [1] and the affine representation found in [2]. These problems achieve conjugacy and establish the validity of the Kuhn-Tucker conditions across the range of these specific scenarios.

Rapidly advancing automated quality control (QC) systems for MRI are driven by the widespread availability of large datasets and robust computational frameworks. Nevertheless, organizations frequently encounter difficulties integrating these systems due to inconsistencies between tools trained on specific datasets and real-world data sources. This study evaluates whether self-organized communities, such as those utilizing wikis, effectively disseminate and maintain algorithms, thereby facilitating the creation of site-specific QC systems. A collection of nine MRI QC algorithms was assembled from the NeuroWiki resource and deployed against current neuroimaging data standards. The results demonstrate that a community-maintained toolkit can facilitate automated flagging data below standards with a median data-point precision of 96.7%. These findings indicate that these sources provide a viable pathway for creating accurate, local automated QC systems.

This research investigates the impact of privately owned electric vehicles on power system stability during disruptions. By introducing a new bi-level optimization framework, our study moves beyond previous limitations that ignored vehicle-to-grid interactions and various outage scenarios. In this new model, the lower level models how private EVs self-organize to seek service during disruptions, while the upper level determines either the initiation of specific line failures or the investment in new switchgears aimed at minimizing total system costs. The upper level accounts for how EVs dynamically select charging stations, whether lines fail suddenly or progressively, and whether outages can be managed. Findings from numerical simulations highlight how the behavior of private EVs and the location of power disruptions significantly influence the robustness of the electrical grid during and after events. These results also illustrate the importance of where grid operators choose to trigger outages or locate switchgears, as well as the value of understanding EVs' charging choices.

Recent work by our group introduced the "Motivation Dynamics" framework, which offers a general mathematical approach for modeling and analyzing the mobile autonomy of self-contained systems, including those with mobile agents like drones and mobile robots. This methodology provides a general design and analysis toolset that enables the construction of agents performing complex, task-driven behaviors while simultaneously providing rigorous guarantees on key autonomy metrics, such as convergence rates for task completion and agents' ability to remain within a specific geographic domain.

In this work, we apply the "Motivation Dynamics" framework specifically to the problem of enabling a single agent to remain within a fixed domain while periodically visiting multiple agents or a finite set of targets. We demonstrate how the framework facilitates the design of autonomous mobile agents that are mathematically guaranteed to converge on timed trajectories for prescribed paths and, more broadly, to complete any finite task sequence within a designated domain with globally bounded timing. These properties are ensured through the implementation of control laws that enforce a dynamics-based motivational structure, which in turn drives the agent along a specific desired set of actions or time-lines.

This study investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn$_3$, CmSn$_3$, and the solid solution Gd$_{1-x}$Cm$_x$Sn$_3$ ($x$ = 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, and 1.00) in both their ground states and mixed valence scenarios. Using the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the Kohn–Sham framework of density functional theory, researchers found that all calculated ground-state configurations for these compounds and mixed valves display metallic behavior. Although no long-range magnetic ordering was identified for the ground states of each, several excited states were discovered featuring different magnetic arrangements, including ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism in both the ferrimagnetic ground state of GdSn3. Specifically, both the total and per-element magnetic moments for GdSn3 were determined to be 3.0 $\mu_B$. The study also evaluated the effects of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) on ground-state properties and examined various excited ground states by adjusting exchange interactions through changes in unit cell parameters and lattice constants. The work concludes by discussing the implications of these findings regarding the chemical behavior of both the light element (Sn) and heavy element (Gd/Cm) within this intermetallic system.

How does your application context influence object detection? Do you look for a specific vehicle type, like a truck, on the road or in a parking lot? In multi-agent systems, collaboration is crucial as it enables task accomplishment beyond individual capabilities. This study introduces a framework modeling such interactions as a multi-agent Markov game, where each agent selects a sub-task execution strategy. We define a sub-task execution policy as a Markov decision process (MDP) specific to that sub-task, where states and transitions are determined by the actions of other agents. Our approach seeks mixed strategy Nash equilibria within this setting to ensure robust performance against the worst possible behaviors of peers. Agents seeking to execute a single sub-task with consistency will find their optimal policies as loops of deterministic actions; we derive the conditions for Nash equilibria formed by such action cycles and present an iterative method to identify them. For scenarios where sub-task execution strategies do not form an equilibrium, we focus on refining strategies to improve performance. Specifically, if policy updates follow best-response dynamics, we prove convergence toward a Nash equilibrium. Additionally, if updates adhere to a broader class of monotone improvement rules, these updates must also lead to convergence. Towards practical application, we define a gradient-based update procedure suitable for continuous and high-dimensional environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SRFF matches or exceeds the performance of both RFF and state-of-the-art random projection methods.

Extra-large MIMO (XL-MIMO) systems, utilizing antennas distributed across an extensive physical area, are emerging as a key solution for maintaining strong radio links in environments with high user density and complex layouts. However, implementing XL-MIMO introduces new challenges regarding the mathematical modeling of array patterns and channel responses. This work addresses these issues by deriving analytical models for XL-MIMO array patterns and wireless channels that accurately reflect practical deployments. Specifically, we evaluate three distinct antenna configurations: a planar XL-MIMO structure, an linear XL-MIMO built from distributed antenna units, and a spherical XL-MIMO composed of multiple spheres. For each setup, the corresponding array pattern and channel response are formulated. Notably, our model for the linear XL-MIMO incorporates a novel, robust calculation for the Walsh-Hadamard pattern in large-scale scenarios to ensure accuracy. Ultimately, the proposed framework offers valuable insights into the design and implementation of real-world XL-MIMO systems.

Although the exact mechanisms behind stellar and planetary disk formation remain unclear, observations of substructures within young stellar disks are ubiquitous. These features include spiral arms, vortices, and gaps. While theories propose that planets or self-gravitating forces drive such structures, it is increasingly recognized that asymmetric heating and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) processes can also generate them. In this work, we present the first observational evidence of heat-driven disk spirals. Using the Submillimeter Array (SMA), we analyzed 24 hours of data to create a high dynamic range, high spatial resolution continuum image at 1.3 mm of the disk around the Herbig Ae star HD 163296. Prominent spiral structures are clearly visible in both the continuum intensity map and dust temperature data. Furthermore, the outer disk's heat pattern exhibits an asymmetric "J-shaped" distribution, the cause of which remains uncertain but has been linked to asymmetric viscous heating in similar systems. Most significantly, detailed dust radiative transfer modeling of the substructure in HD 163296 confirms that heat-driven instabilities are the most plausible explanation for these observations. While ruling out other potential causes—such as localized dust emission, localized accretion, or localized planet formation remains challenging due to limited data—current constraints strongly suggest a planetary origin for the embedded structure seen in previous studies of HD 163296.

The nature of the second compact object involved in the GW190814 event remains a key unresolved issue, with final analyses of its characteristics from the analysis of the gravitational waves remaining limited to general findings. However, the recent discovery of the 2.60 $M_{\odot}$ neutron star in the optical afterglow provides a definitive minimum mass limit for this component. By utilizing this established lower bound mass alongside an upper limit of 2.68 $M_{\odot}$ derived from the analysis of the radiation from the remnant, we have determined the feasible ranges for several key features of this star. Specifically, its radius must lie between 10.8 and 14.1 kilometers, the equation of state permitting such a massive core permits a maximum neutron number of at least $1.72\times 10^{57}$ but no more than $1.77\times 10^{57}$, the star's age must be at least $1.12\times 10^5$ years old, and the surface magnetic field strength must range from $1.16\times 10^{21}$ to $1.23\times 10^{21}$ Gauss.

This study presents the design and implementation of frequency-robust Mølmer–Sørensen gates for a linear trapped ion architecture, utilizing Gaussian amplitude modulation coupled with a fixed laser frequency. We chose this single parameterset for optimization specifically to counteract small detuning errors in the interaction frequency, thereby enhancing resilience against such variations. This targeted approach contrasts with commonly used methods that achieve robustness through timing precision or multiple frequencies, both of which are limited by how accurately the motional mode can be characterized. Experiments demonstrate stable two-ion gate fidelities exceeding 99.2% across varying populations of four to twelve ions extending over a three-meter distance.

The Dirac cones found in graphene possess linear dispersion relations composed of electron states, which restricts the scope of interaction-driven phenomena. We demonstrate that incorporating simple, light-hole valence band effects—also present with linear dispersion but composed of both electron and hole components—can lift these limitations. Specifically, we focus on graphene on a substrate with broken time-reversal symmetry (TRS), such as those exhibiting the anomalous Hall effect (AHE). In this context, inter-electronic interactions linked to the AHE arise exclusively from holes, whereas in the standard case of graphene on free space, they originate from both electrons and holes. We show that interplay between the interplay of these factors and inter-band scattering generates an instability toward a hole-driven AHE in pure graphene, violating the cancellation of AHE that typically occurs when electrons, holes, and linear dispersion interact. We also examine the implications of our results regarding light-induced phenomena, specifically the generation of mass in Dirac electrons.

Heavy neutral leptons (HNLS) are a generic feature of seesaw models and represent a compelling source of CP violation and additional contributions to electroweak symmetry breaking. Their significance is characterized by the mixing angle $|U_e|^2$. This study investigates the constraints imposed by electron scattering experiments in Earth's core and solar interior, specifically focusing on how these datasets limit mixing angles associated with mass scales around the TeV level. We examine two distinct HNLS scenarios: a single heavy neutral leptos with real 4×N Dirac mass matrices and a pair of heavy neutral leptos forming a second-seesaw model. Our analysis demonstrates that electron recoil data can significantly weaken bounds on $|U_e|^2$ derived from HNLS explanations of disjoint physical phenomena, such as anomalous magnetic moments of the muon or tau lepton, or unexpected electron fluxes from solar and supernova sources.

Although neural language models have achieved significant success and are now prevalent in numerous commercial applications, $N$-gram models remain a viable alternative, specifically when dealing with low-volume target languages where limited data prevents neural networks from effectively learning linguistic patterns. To address this scenario for such low-resource languages, we introduce $N$yuro, a hybrid framework designed to enhance the generation capabilities of $N$-gram by integrating the statistical power derived from vast English corpus with the specific vocabulary of your target language. In our approach, the source (target) component is extracted from textual data within the target language corpus, whereas the target (English) component originates from massive English corpus. To address differences in lexical structure, we apply a dynamic translation process to the target $N$-gram sources so they align with the specificities of the English corpus used for training. In our experiments, employing the $N$yuro approach for generation on the Turkish language corpus resulted in a 0.4 increase in human preferred generation for the Turkish language. Additionally, we observed a 0.4 improvement in the human preferred generation of the Turkish language using the same model on a smaller corpus. The specific $N$yuro model achieved these results using just 1 million words of training data, demonstrating significant performance gains compared to standard neural approaches using the same amount of data.

Accurately reconstructing and aligning faces in 3D--even those plagued by occlusions and extreme expressions--poses a formidable challenge, particularly when combined with non-trivial camera conditions. Our approach introduces a novel framework grounded in implicit neural representations, specifically the signed distance function (SDF), augmented with an orientation term to simultaneously handle occlusion and visibility. This method encodes both robust geometric details and appearance data, while our training strategy incorporates a masking scheme designed to navigate the complexities of occlusion and various head orientations. Furthermore, the model ensures realistic reconstruction by integrating physical constraints that govern both surface topology and light behavior, such as occluding contours and self-occlusions. We validate the effectiveness of this pipeline through extensive experiments, demonstrating that it reliably rebuilds and correctly aligns faces in challenging real-world images containing occlusions, heavy noise, and diverse poses.

Utilizing a linear perturbation analysis in an inflationary model featuring a coupling between the inflaton and curvature modulation fields, we demonstrate that conditions in the primordial universe favorable for generating a significant abundance of primordial black holes—specifically those with initial densities exceeding linear perturbations around $10^{14}\mathrm{g}$--coexist with early universe phase transitions. These predictions align with current constraints derived from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, stellar galactic dynamics, solar system dynamics, and the lack of detected radio transients, collectively indicating a forbidden parameter space for PBHs with masses between $10^{14}\mathrm{g}$ and $10^{19}\mathrm{g}$.

Storage is vital for providing the ancillary services needed to stabilize electricity prices and enable a renewable energy system. This paper presents a review of risk storage strategies, with a specific focus on how storage operators respond to price volatility. Our analysis indicates that risk-averse behavior causes storage resources to withhold capacity when prices are high and release it when prices are low, effectively reversing the flow of electricity and reducing generationists' profits. These outcomes carry significant implications for system reliability and question whether risk-based storage policies can truly support a sustainable, renewable power grid.

We utilize a three-dimensional general circulation model (GCM) to investigate the development and characteristics of baroclinic atmospheres surrounding planetary bodies with varying levels of spin. Our focus is on identifying the critical conditions under which multiple atmospheric jets emerge. Our study reveals a strong dependence of jet formation on both the mass and rotational velocity of the planet. Specifically, low-mass, slowly rotating environments tend to support only solitary jets positioned at the equator. Conversely, high-mass or rapidly rotating systems foster the creation of multiple jets distributed across diverse latitudes. This latter phenomenon arises because Rossby waves—generated by the breakdown of baroclinic instability—generate absolute vorticity gradients capable of counteracting the planetary Coriolon effect further poleward. Ultimately, the number of jets is dictated by the spacing of these latitudinal zones of absolute vorticity minima. We demonstrate this framework through applications to current Earth-like scenarios, including the comparison of present-day Earth and the high-pressure atmosphere of Venus.

We propose an alternative approach that merges self-supervised pretraining with active learning to identify samples for labeling that most enhance model performance after full dataset training with unlabeled data. We analyze the transport characteristics of HgTe quantum wells with critical thickness, a regime where the band gap closes and the low-energy spectrum typically involves Dirac states protected by helical edge modes. Within a semi-classical framework, we derive these quantum anomalous Hall (Dirac) states using an effective massive Dirac model and identify the mechanism generating these helical states as the inversion of the low-energy bulk dispersion relation under an applied magnetic field. Specifically, the field shifts the Fermi arc across the quantum anomalous Hall spectrum, creating a scenario analogous to the integer quantum Hall effect but without Landau level quantization of the bulk. However, this same quantum wells exhibit distinct magnetic breakdown phenomena that contradict the standard quantum anomalous Hall predictions. These effects stem from the formation of non-hyperbolic, parabolic "magnetic Dirac" states. Consequently, these findings clarify previous experimental ambiguities regarding HgTe quantum wells intended to host quantum anomalous Hall behavior.

Dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) allows each base station to schedule uplink and downlink transmissions independently according to its own traffic load. Unfortunately, this decentralization leads to intercell cross-interference, making the combined problem of resource allocation and power control computationally difficult (NP-hard). To address this, we formulate the dynamic TDD resource allocation challenge as a mixed integer non-linear programming problem. Furthermore, we introduce two novel algorithms, the Distributed Dynamic TDD Algorithm (DDTA) and the Distributed Dynamic TDD Algorithm with Improved Iteration (DDTA-II), to efficiently solve it. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our proposed approaches significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a meta-learning algorithm utilizing ODE-based neural networks that explicitly learn gradient relationships. By equipping optimizers with learned gradients, this method introduces a flexible architecture and an inherent inductive bias toward optimization, enabling a trade-curve of solutions ranging from low to high numbers of few-shot shots. specifically focused on few-shot image classification, the use of continuous differentiability allows the application of differential equation solving techniques, resulting in a multi-objective trade-curve. The use of differential equation neural (DENO) networks helps learn this multi-objective trade-curve, and evidence shows that this approach can outperform the best few (or single) solution found so far. Computational experiments provide evidence that this multi-objective approach can achieve a better few-shot image classification performance compared to the best traditional optimization result.

Enhanced model accuracy alone is insufficient; building trustworthy AI is equally crucial for creating resilient systems in high-stakes fields like healthcare, automotive, and finance. We introduce a hybrid multi-agent framework integrating human and computational agents to address this. In our setup, a skeptical human agent acts as an auditor who challenges a probabilistic AI agent claiming responsibility for a real-time, secure AI function. While the AI continuously improves its accuracy, the human increases confidence in the model by adjusting her reliance based on her recent track record with that specific output. We evaluate this framework using a convolutional neural network agent against various "black box" adversarial agents. Our findings demonstrate that this trust calibration mechanism not only boosts the model's robustness against attacks but also significantly improves system reliability.

This study concentrates on two pivotal aspects of cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing, namely schema linking and argument extraction. We suggest a novel column selection auxiliary task designed to bridge the schema linking process in semantic parsing across domains. Empirical tests conducted on the Spider benchmark demonstrate significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods, with further analysis offering insights into these model capabilities and performance.

This paper investigates the deployment of differential privacy (DP) within graph-structured environments. It examines various DP formulations tailored to different privacy threats in graph environments, including graph isomorphism, membership inference, and background knowledge. Although prior research has focused on DP techniques for tabular and other domains, these approaches are poorly suited for graph-related attributes, particularly the intricate graph-to-graph mapping required for most graph algorithms. Furthermore, existing methods often fail to adequately address specific graph privacy risks. To mitigate these issues, the authors propose a unified and broadly applicable differential private graph framework (DPGF). This framework addresses multiple Dp formulations by integrating a privacy-preserving graph rewriting mechanism, thereby transforming different datasets into graphs that enable private information aggregation and analysis on tabular data.

The vast array of data, images, and resources Euclid will provide—boasting 1-metre-square kilometres of optical clarity—necessitate next-generation processing pipelines to ensure the array's full potential is realized. Although the planned end-to-end simulation framework employs fully rendered cubic gigabyte-rendered (RGB) renderings to replicate the realistic instrument effects and physical phenomena anticipated by the upcoming mission, the forthcoming live scientific datasets will exist primarily in the compact real-space formats optimized for both spectral analysis and imaging. Rather than simply re-running the current render within these simulated datasets, a more feasible strategy for generating high-fidelity views and tunes from actual data involves developing transfer functions that replicate the visual signatures found within the realistic end-to-end renderings when applied to data in its compact format. To support this initiative, we present a transfer of our realistic simulation framework's gains by developing and releasing these necessary rendering parameters. Concurrently, we introduce a prototype pipeline capable of applying such transfers to generate high-fidelity visualizations directly from the output of end-to-end renderings. This approach not only yields visuals indistinguishable in quality from those of the original simulations but also ensures a processing time that scales efficiently with the size of the actual dataset. Furthermore, this method guarantees a faithful representation of the intricate spectral linearity inherent in the data. Ultimately, this enhanced imaging protocol will maximize the scientific impact of Euclid's one-square-meter-kilometre images and spectra across all future galaxy evolution analyses.

K-fold cross-validation serves as the primary method for evaluating and adjusting machine learning models; however, its high computational cost—necessitating the complete retraining of models for every evaluation point—often limits practical application. Although this overhead is acceptable for smaller datasets, it becomes prohibitive on large data volumes, as even a single training run demands substantial time and resources.

To address this, we, and others previously, proposed using a subset of data for the efficient parameter selection within K-fold cross-validation. The rationale is that key hyperparameters can typically be identified by training on data subsets, with the assumption that such parameters remain effective when applied to the full dataset for performance assessment.

We propose the Batched Cross-Validation with Subsets (BCVS) algorithm, which employs Batchknn to efficiently identify optimal hyperparameters using subset data. BCVS integrates two innovations: (1) the utilization of BatchKNN for rapid performance estimation based on prior literature, and (2) a streamlined workflow requiring only one implementation of the data partitioning process.

Experiments conducted on three datasets using a LightGBM classifier confirm that the proposed subset-based strategies successfully identify hyperparameters performing on par with those found via traditional, computationally expensive K-fold cross-validation.

Intelligent knowledge networks, built upon diverse architectures like Acyclic Graphs (KNGs) and Neural Networks (KNNGs), constitute a primary focus in international research. Recent advances in "collaborative learning" and "knowledge distillation" have introduced Teacher-Student frameworks to enhance these systems with new insights. In "collaborative learning," multiple students compete to learn from one another's guidance, with the most competent model selected as the superior source of knowledge. Similarly, "knowledge distillation" functions as a Teacher-student dynamic, where the refined expertise of the teacher is transferred to the student to enhance performance. Both "collaborative learning" and "knowledge distillation" are emerging as prominent strategies within intelligent knowledge systems, facilitating more efficient system evolution through shared expertise and refined understanding. However, current methodologies often lack robust mechanisms for accurately evaluating the depth of knowledge transfer and the quality of insights contributed by peers. To address this gap, we introduce a novel framework known as "Knowledge Apprenticeship." This approach employs a rigorous teacher-student architecture designed to measure, evaluate, and optimize the learning process through quantifiable knowledge assessments and student performance analysis using distinct evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we have developed an innovative evaluation metric specifically for knowledge models to track student advancement. The superiority and practical applicability of Knowledge Apprenticeship have been validated through extensive experiments comparing it against state-of-the-art baselines on both synthetic data and real-world datasets.

This paper introduces a new compact representation method for graphical models, called DA-FG. It combines deterministic finite state automata (for encoding valid input sequences) with edge-subgraphs (for managing non-linear feature dependencies). Equipped with this approach, Visions4Action can effectively build and operate various types of graphical models. Furthermore, the utilization of finite state automata allows for a significant decrease in the number of configurations, facilitating more effective exact inference.

Dense suspensions experience a non-linear increase in viscosity under high shear stress, a phenomenon known as the inertial thinning transition. While the resulting shear profile displays an apparent yield stress, its shape varies with suspension viscosity and the applied stress level. Despite extensive research, the fundamental mechanisms governing the transition from thin to thick behavior at elevated stresses have remained unclear. The present work presents viscosity measurements utilizing particle image velocimetry (PIV) for various dense aluminum oxide suspensions. PIV data for aluminum oxide suspensions reveal that the balance of normal forces shifts during transition from particle inertia to normal stress gradients caused by viscosity variations. This realignment leads to radial particle migration, elevating volume fractions near the pipe walls while depleting them at the center. These discoveries, derived specifically through PIV analysis, rely on viscous normal stresses and particle inertia as the primary drivers for the shift from thick to thick rheological states in dense aluminum oxide suspensions.

Personalization of web search represents a significant obstacle to securing relevant information for critical tasks, such as obtaining medical advice or locating reliable information on viruses. Although researchers have investigated the resulting relevance gaps, there remains limited understanding of the extent to which this tailoring occurs and the specific mechanisms employed. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of personalization across three widely used search engines—Bing, Google, and Yahoo!—by systematically manipulating various query attributes. Our experimental approach involved manually constructing a dataset of 1,000 significant, non-routinely searched topics spanning language learning, virus prevention, and diet and nutrition. By altering the background, device, location, and device of the searcher for each topic, we measured differences in results. Our findings reveal that Google and Yahoo! clearly prioritize personalization, whereas Bing exhibits minimal tailoring. Furthermore, both Google and Yahoo! were found to forgo approximately one page of highly relevant content due to this effect, indicating that web search personalization can potentially overlook over 20% of top-relevant information.

**Objective:** This study aims to develop and evaluate a free-breathing T2-weighted MRI sequence utilizing RARE with variable flip angles (RARE-VF) enhanced by dynamic k-space sampling to mitigate respiratory artifacts.

**Methods:** In RARE-VF, non-Cartian k-space trajectories enable the customization of contrast by adjusting fill factor patterns and their arrangements. The proposed technique involves a specific k-space filling sequence designed to concentrate high spatial resolution in areas least affected by respiratory motion. Parameters were optimized using simulated trapezoidal signal decay envelopes resulting from breathing-induced volume fluctuations. Subsequently, the dynamic k-space ordering, contrast integrity, and through-plane resolution were assessed through simulations and in vivo experiments using both intentionally induced respiratory movements and free-breathing scans.

**Results:** Simulations demonstrated that a variable trace of fill factor adjustments—aggressive near the center of k-space and gradual toward the edges—can generate center shifts of 1.0 cm or more due to breathing while sustaining high-quality images. Furthermore, the designated time-varying k-space trajectory successfully preserved contrast characteristics and through-plane sharpness in T2 RARE-VF images, even with large unconstrained breathing volumes in vivo.

**Conclusion:** The proposed dynamic k-space sampling strategy effectively minimizes respiratory distortion in free-breathing T2 RARE-VF imaging by situating high-resolution encoding in the part of the trajectory least susceptible to breathing-related motion.

This study introduces a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that employs a grid-based strategy for target birth and undetected target intensities. While the intensity of first-time detected targets is approximated using a single Gaussian distribution, the intensity of currently undetected targets within each cell is handled via the formulation of the characteristic function of the Riemman-Stieltz (RSMF) based intensity characteristic function. Although conventional approaches utilize Gaussian distributions, this method offers a significant computational advantage by eschewing the typical high-dimensional mixtures required to represent arbitrary intensities; instead of Gaussian components, it uses discrete, grid-based steps. The key benefit of this gird-intensity RSMBM (GIG) is that filters can accurately handle the intensity of targets, even with the high-dimensional and complex nature of the system without the heavy use of computational resources. The gird intensity (GI) of the target, along with the ability to effectively manage the complex and variable intensity targets, makes the filter a promising approach. Soccer is a sparsely rewarded game where strategic choices during pivotal moments heavily influence whether a team secures victory or defeat. Focusing on whether a soccer team should press for a goal or settle for a draw in critical phases, this study frames the sport as an infinite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP) to identify and locate such crucial states within an MDP structure and develop state features relevant to these areas. We also establish an optimal MDP policy to compare proposed techniques against existing methods. However, due to the resulting optimal policy's excessive complexity, the paper introduces two new, suggested policies that are both highly performant and easy to implement. Extensive simulations using real-world data to validate these approaches demonstrate significant performance improvements over current state-of-the-art methods.

Full waveform inversion (FWI), which enhances initial subsurface models by contrasting synthetic with observed data, frequently encounters difficulties due to the computationally intensive generation of wavefields required to achieve convergence on a refined Earth model. Wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) addresses this challenge by utilizing stored forward simulation data through a combination of synthetic checkpoints and mathematical backward propagators known as propagators. The feasibility of WRI relies on solving for these propagators as an optimization problem so that stored check-point data can be extrapolated both temporally and spatially to recreate the complete forward waveform field. This study demonstrates the application of a new WRI method that reconstructs these propagators using a reduced set of temporal checkpoints during standard frequency-domain finite-difference simulations. By minimizing a misfit function defined against available synthetic snapshots at these reduced checkpoints, this approach facilitates the misfit necessary to make back-propagation feasible without requiring continuous or complete initial pressure fields. Employable within a multi-scale framework, this reduced-checkpoint WRI method offers a practical avenue for implementing WRI using existing workflow tools.

This study presents our novel "Immigration-Space Competition Model" (iSCM), a framework designed to explore how immigration influences ecological dynamics, specifically how immigrant species compete with established communities. The core of the new model involves a dynamic vector of densities for $N$ coexisting species, where density at any given location is determined by an interplay between immigration rates, intraspecific regulation, and interspecific interactions. We analyze the model through two perspectives: a local view, which investigates whether an incoming species can invade an established species' territory, and a global view, which examines whether an immigrant group can establish itself within the existing community structure. The results offer ecological insights into the complex relationship between immigration rates and competitive outcomes, revealing that the ability of an immigrant to establish depends on whether it can dominate its regulator. Furthermore, the model clarifies why high immigration rates can lead to lower diversity, demonstrating their dual role in driving both invasion and extinction events. This approach provides a coherent mechanism for interpreting the intricate connections between immigration rates, species diversity, and competitive displacement.

Because the magnitude and direction of the YORP torque fluctuate based on an object's shape, size, and thermal properties, predicting the spin evolution of specific asteroids remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a streamlined method for approximating the YORP torque on irregularly shaped asteroids by modeling spin axes perpendicular to their largest inertia principal axis as equivalent to those of a spinning top in uniform gravity. In this framework, solar radiation pressure functions as the "gravitational" force, with its unit vector denoted as $\odot$. The resulting dimensionless torque depends on the solar direction relative to the object, defined by two angles $\theta$ and $\theta'$, and two dimensionless parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that relate to size and thermal characteristics. This $\beta$-parameterized "spin top" approach is applied to the spin evolution predictions of various asteroids, including Mathilde, 2001 DA, 2001 FO, and 2001 FO, and an object with similar structure to an asteroid.

While neuroscientists generally agree that the ventral visual cortex (VVC) exhibits a gradient in responding to living things versus non-living things, two years apart, two hypotheses explain this "animacy continuum." The first hypothesis suggests the continuum reflects feedforward information flow concerning life status; we tested this by examining the relationship between response continuum slopes and the timing of feedforward connections. The opposing hypothesis posits that the gradient arises from feedback connections. We developed a novel model to test both proposals, one that generates the animacy response continuum solely through its feedforward architecture. Our model demonstrates that both feedforward and feedback structures could account for the continuum, yet our findings indicate that its feedforward properties are more critical and that feedback properties alone are insufficient explanation. Finally, the article concludes by suggesting future experiments designed specifically to evaluate these hypotheses.

Super-spreader incidents frequently hasten the progression of infectious outbreaks. Analyzing their impact remains vital for accurately modeling epidemic dynamics and refining forecasts. This study investigates whether such events exert a reduction or enhancement on the effective reproductive rate ($R_e$). Findings reveal that holding the basic reproductive rate ($R_0$) constant, varying the distribution of transmission heterogeneity alters the effective reproductive rate ($R_e$). Specifically, the effective basic reproductive rate ($R_e$) varies based on whether an outbreak is in its early stages or advanced phases. In summary, both the timing of super-spreader occurrences within an outbreak and the fundamental reproductive rate ($R_0$) determine whether the effective basic reproductive rate ($R_e$) increases or decreases.

The paper addresses the bias affecting the measurement of the magnetic field component perpendicular to the line-of-sight ($B_{\perp}$) within weak-to-moderate fields, utilizing the Total Solar Magnetic Flux (TSFM) technique. Additionally, the text applies this model to analyze $B_{\perp}$ biases in fields containing Gaussian noise and those with prominent magnetic features like sunspots. Key influences on this specific bias include magnetogram coverage area, field orientation, and granulation patterns. Finally, the text explores the resulting systematic errors in fields of origin analysis, concluding that the negative impact is minimal, particularly when combined with other existing sources of uncertainty.

Beginning in January 2020, the H7N9 bird flu epidemic in China sparked widespread online misinformation, with related posts reaching over 10 million views within 72 hours and generating more than 100,000 comments. This study examines the underlying mechanisms of such information cascades by reconstructing an epistemic network from one day of Weibo data—China's primary social platform—which offers insights applicable to other systems. Analysis reveals these rumor outbreaks follow a biphasic pattern: an initial surge driven by anticipation, followed by a secondary wave fueled by engagement (such as comments and reposts). While the host of the epidemic explains the initial spread, it does not account for the subsequent phase. Furthermore, findings indicate the phenomenon exhibits significant resilience against standard content-deletion moderation. Consequently, the authors argue that standard interventions are insufficient and propose that introducing targeted counter-deception narratives may effectively curb the spread of online misinformation during public health emergencies.

Planetary Nebulae (PNe) serve as valuable "standard candles" for measuring distances to their host galaxies. However, the reliability of this technique is constrained by uncertainties in determining ages and extinction values, alongside the difficulty in identifying the individual H$\alpha$ emission components that constitute the complex spectra of PN. Recent advances in analyzing these H$\alpha$ profiles, utilizing the high-resolution data from the Gemini South High Resolution Spectrograph (GSHRS), have enabled the construction of detailed models for several prominent PNe in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). These models successfully replicate the H$\alpha$ structure of specific objects, including NGC 3132 ("The Trifid"), NGC 3167 ("The Dumbbell"), NGC 3197 ("The Fox Fur Trapper"), NGC 3226 ("The Bug"), NGC 3293 ("The Pacman"), and NGC 3324 ("The Southern Rose"). Although this approach provides valuable insights into the morphology and kinematics of these well-known LMC objects, its application to precisely determine the Large Magellanic Cloud's distance remains limited when compared to other established methods.

Healthcare providers, researchers, and individuals alike rely on physiological data streams to analyze medical trends and enhance diagnostic capabilities for conditions such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes. Unfortunately, existing streaming technologies are plagued by excessive latency, cumbersome development workflows, and prohibitively high costs. To address these challenges, we introduce LifeStream, a dedicated service for handling biomedical data streams that delivers a lightweight interface, near-real-time processing capabilities, and an affordable operational model. Complementing this, the BioGraph Library offers a comprehensive suite of tools designed for stream-based biomedical signal processing. Evaluations demonstrate that operations on streams containing one terabyte of data take only a fraction of a second using LifeStream with BioGraph, highlighting its superior efficiency over current solutions.

The loss function stands as one of the most crucial hyperparameters in a neural network, and with the myriad of designs available, selecting the correct one remains challenging. This work focuses specifically on classification with deep neural networks using supervised data, where the study examines how the influence of the loss function interacts with the underlying data distribution. The research evaluates the effects of different losses within a categorical data framework, utilizing categorical targets encoded via one-hot scheme. The key finding reveals that while prior studies often report superior performance of specific non-standard losses, this advantage frequently disappears when the true label is known and the original categorical label is utilized for training with cross-validation using a standard softmax output and cross-entropy training. The study notes that this performance parity exists because the one-hot encoded target already represents a valid 0/1 distribution, which aligns perfectly with the implicit probabilistic model of the standard neural network. The findings suggest that for supervised classification with 0/1 distributions, the implicit probability model of the standard soft-max already provides the optimal performance, which is why the standard cross-entropy is the optimal choice of loss.

Conventional non-coherent differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM) demonstrates significant robustness against channel impairments like phase and Doppler shifts. Furthermore, this implementation remains simple, primarily requiring the lookup of a conventional coherent detection result. However, this traditional differential method suffers from a key drawback: differential encoding effectively converts narrow-band CPM into linearly modulated signaling, causing the spectral efficiency to drop proportionally to the CPM's rolling bandwidth constraint. This study introduces a novel non-coherent differential detection algorithm that is compatible with non-linear CPM constellations, achieving the reversal of narrow-band spectral characteristics without compromising the conventional coherent detection performance. Consequently, the presented approach generalizes existing conventional differential detection, which handles linear CPM constellations, and improves upon it by preserving full narrow-band spectral efficiency.

The Feynman-Jarnik inequality allows for the characterization of intensive parameters within intensive systems. In this work, we apply this principle to quasi-equilibrant one-dimensional scattering systems to demonstrate that variations in the local Fisher information information regarding the mean energy are constrained. Specifically, in the non-degenerate regime, these fluctuations of the local energy are frequency-scale invariant. As a consequence, the Fisher information information concerning the energy density is also confined. We further present an explicit representation showing that the variance of the local energy is proportional to the product of the energy density squared. Additionally, there exists a direct connection between the variance of the local energy and the local energy density in location one-dimensional scattering systems.

Introducing ATOMIC is an extensive commonsense reasoning framework comprising 877,000 textual examples of inferential knowledge, distinguishing itself from current resources that primarily rely on taxonomies, ATOMIC concentrates on typed if‑then rules featuring variables (such as "if one apologizes to someone for wrongdoing, they may subsequently offer that person assistance"). Achieving complementary goals, ATOMIC aims to supply training material suited for learning causal reasoning and distinction, whereas other resources seek to facilitate computational natural language generation, natural language inference, and question‑answering tasks. Our framework involves annotators constructing if‑then statements from over 1 million unique inferential patterns; each statement is then used to generate continuation sentences which are annotated with a relevance score and a specific category label. The resulting dataset features deepRelevance and a semantic category tag for every text pair. Our framework also provides automated generation of continuation texts based on initial input sentences, and human evaluators assessed the resulting data quality. Our framework showed that large language models trained exclusively on this material learned 93.9% inference and could generalize these lessons to novel questions with high accuracy. Our framework highlights the value of explicit inferential training material and establishes a resource that enables advanced AI systems to learn complex logical relationships.

Although vital for finance, the computational complexity of classical portfolio optimization algorithms prompts finance technology companies to develop algorithms for faster hardware. While approximations work for some financial data, using quantum algorithms like HHL to solve this optimization for real data without approximation is more beneficial. The HHL algorithm offers exponential speedups for linear system solving, yet its practical use remains unclear. This study provides the first implementation details for HHL in portfolio optimization, outlining specific requirements and performance metrics. We analyze the algorithm's input needs, data processing, and output interpretation to demonstrate how finance professionals can utilize it. Speed tests and comparisons with classical methods highlight the necessary conditions and potential applications of this quantum approach in finance.

This paper proposes new data augmentation strategies to enhance the data efficiency of end-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models trained via multimodal methods, targeting two key areas in Microsoft's OneASR architecture: (1) improved frame-level alignment between audio and text and (2) more accurate character generation from aligned sequences. First, we introduce a text-informed augmentation technique that diversifies training text while preserving semantic integrity, specifically designed to address the alignment challenge. Second, we present a noise-informed augmentation method for audio that enriches the training sounds without altering textual content, thereby facilitating better generation. Evaluations on the OneASR model demonstrate that these approaches effectively improve data efficiency in the multimodal training process, resulting in higher quality audio-to-text alignments and more accurate speech generation.

Our research investigates the asymptotic behavior ($n \to \infty$) of the initial $k_n$ components of a stochastic uniform parking function of length $n$ (where $0 < k_n < n$). We observe that these components, when scaled by $1/n$ and arranged in order, converge to the configuration of deterministic uniform parking functions of infinite length under the uniform distribution. Specifically, for any fixed integer $i \ge 1$, the expected value of the $i$-th component in this limit process is precisely the natural density of requests required to achieve a deterministic parking outcome of length $n$ as that determinant size approaches infinity, as established by Dykstra (1974). Furthermore, we derive results regarding the joint distribution of these initial components. Additionally, we demonstrate that the first component's fluctuations around its mean scale according to a $\log(\log(n))$ rate, contrasting with the $\log(n)$ scaling seen in deterministic cases. Finally, we establish a central limit theorem applicable to the initial components when $k_n$ allows for significant variability.

The $\Omega^{-}$, composed of three strange quarks ($sss$), is a good testing ground for understanding the role of spin and flavor structure in heavily strange hadrons. In this work, we apply our in-medium effective quark model to examine the electromagnetic form factors of the $\Omega$ in relation to its radius and shape. Specifically, we calculate the vector current form factors, $F_C$ and $F_M$, for the $\Omega$ by utilizing the double line diagram technique within the model framework. Our results indicate values of $\sqrt{r^2_\Omega}$ approximately 0.4 fm greater than those observed for the proton. Specifically, $r^2_\Omega \approx 0.9$ fm larger than the proton radius, with numerical findings of $r^2_\Omega \approx 0.36$ fm and $r^2_\Omega \approx 0.40$ fm under different coupling scenarios, implying $\Omega$ radius values around 0.8 fm and 0.84 fm respectively. These results suggest the $\Omega$ is significantly less bound compared to other hadrons containing fewer strange quarks. Additionally, since our model inherently accounts for both connected and disconnected quark loop structures, we extract information regarding disconnected loops from the ratio of calculated to measured form factors, finding a disconnected connected quark loop (DC) contribution of roughly 15%.

Air transmission of infectious agents occurs through virus-carrying aerosols interacting with turbulent fluid flows; therefore, understanding spatial transmission requires examining particle physics within various enclosed environments. This study investigates the stochastic dynamics of such particles using a population of viral-laden aerosols in a car parking garage. We analyze how spatial distribution is influenced by particle physics and environmental control variables, specifically comparing uncontrolled conditions to those with an active HEPA filtration system. Our findings indicate that under normal circumstances, infection-carrying particles accumulate in parking garage corners, a phenomenon that remains significant even when HEPA systems are installed and operating.

The Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC) induced proximity effect has become a significant area of research in condensed matter physics. This work demonstrates that the inclusion of lattice anharmonicity in multilayer systems can substantially elevate SOC even near interfaces with high-orbit materials. Furthermore, we find that interlayer interactions leading to heightened OAM include not only orbital hybridization but also charge and magnetic moment transfer. These discoveries offer new avenues for manipulating orbital degrees of freedom and expanding the proximity-induced SOC in ultrathin films near interfaces with high-OAM materials.

This study explores imposing explicit Lipschitz constraints on neural network architectures to ensure stable dynamics with bounded input changes. We introduce a novel method for calculating an upper limit of the Lipschitz constant for the entire network and utilize it as a training objective. Results indicate that neural networks trained via our approach exhibit significantly improved input robustness compared to standard contrastive learning, while maintaining similar contrastive losses.
