The theoretical framework addressing recent anomalies in lepton-flavour non-universality at the $Z_{\rm boson}$ and meson decays involves vector leptoquarks with a mass scale near 1 TeV. This study investigates the possibility of explaining the proton-proton collision anomalies via a specific interaction between quark and lepton triplets that do not serve as vector leptoquarks. By analysing the same-proper time dilepton and different-proper time patterns within the context of various $g_{3L}$-vector leptoquark scenarios, we observe that the required interaction strengths and the non-universal third-generation lepton branching ratios of the $g_{3L}$-vector leptoquark are inconsistent with the proton-proton collision data. Furthermore, the $g_{3L}$-vector leptoquark model predicts specific correlations among the $Z_{\rm boson}$ and the non-universal third-generation lepton branching ratios that contradict current experimental measurements. Additionally, the non-universal third-generation lepton requirements of the $g_{3L}$-vector leptoquark model face stringent constraints from proton-proton searches targeting non-standard neutral currents. Finally, the potential for future experiments to clarify the nature of the non-universal third-generation lepton requirements imposed by the non-$g_{3L}$-vector leptoquark model is explored through proton-proton searches for non-standard neutral currents.

Radiation concerns limit the clinical use of positron emission tomography (PET) scans for vulnerable groups such as pregnant women and children. Radiation dose does not determine image quality, as quality is constrained by the minimum detectable effect size. We argue that dose reduction is not the primary solution; rather, research must prioritize enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) while maintaining acceptable increases in image contrast. We evaluate two existing research frameworks that focus on the smallest detectable change in image density. Both models rely on change detection theory and utilize an F-test based on log image intensities, assuming both groups contain an equal number of subjects. The first approach presumes subjects in each group are mutually independent, whereas the second allows for dependencies within subgroups by incorporating a mixed-effects model. We present solutions for both models that require no distributional assumptions regarding the image data, as both proposed frameworks are likelihood-Cramer Rao lower bound (CLRL) unbiased and consistent, with the version for correlated data also being asymptotically normal. A new model extends these methods by addressing small cohorts found in experimental settings; this new framework assumes the presence of correlated data. All three models can be applied regardless of distributional assumptions, as they are both non-parametric and robust. Simulation studies and real-world experiments demonstrate that our proposed model performs as well as current techniques when handling independent data, while clearly surpassing them when analyzing correlated datasets.

Centering theory examines how the structural coherence of discourse emerges through the interaction of consecutive sentences. While the original framework was designed for short, human conversational exchanges, it has since been extended to analyze longer text types, though most existing versions rely on manual annotation and often fail to incorporate semantic information. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a new computational model for building the Centering System (CS) within a fully automated pipeline working across various text corpora. Building upon current state-of-the-art discourse tagging methods, our approach defines specific criteria for applying centering rules and utilizes simple heuristic strategies to construct a functional system capable of accurately forecasting the most promising contentions of dialogue text.

WiFi fingerprints, which utilize collected Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) references to identify specific locations, represent a widely adopted indoor positioning approach. This study introduces a novel contribution: a lightweight, robust, and efficient intra- and inter-cell indoor positioning method based on a newly devised Weighted Nearest Neighbor (WNN) algorithm. Extensive simulations and real-world experiments validate the efficacy of the proposed framework, demonstrating that it achieves horizontal and vertical positioning accuracy of approximately one meter and 50 centimeters, respectively, with only 1000 data points required for each cell.

The Odeh-Ferbrahman-Davidchak-Pincus (OFDP) theory, originally formulated for planar substrates, has been extended in the present research to include monolayers of polyelectrolyte brushes grown on curved surfaces, such as cylinders and spheres. The central objective of the OFDP framework is to model the end exclusion zones of tethered chains, a factor that becomes critical when the average attachment spacing is comparable to the brush thickness. In the case of brush layers on monovalent electrolyte solutions, the theory integrates the energy components of tether stretching, electrostatic interactions, and counterion entropy. The present work demonstrates the successful application of the OFDP model to derive analytical expressions for the vertical profile, scaling dependencies, and morphological characteristics of brushes on both cylindrical and spherical geometries. Additionally, these theoretical predictions have been utilized to analyze the structural transitions of polyelectrolyte monolayers tethered to the inner walls of channels (cylindrical) and on the surfaces of liquid droplets or vesicles (spherical). By comparing stretching, electrostatic, and entropic contributions across planar, curved, and Donnan potential contexts, the paper offers a comprehensive overview of the mechanics governing polyelectrolyte brushes operating in monovalent electrolyte environments.

Inspired by the efficacy of the serial dictatorship mechanism in achieving high utility for individual agents in combinatorial optimization, we analyze its performance relative to total social utility in scenarios involving interdependent valuations and strategic behavior by multiple players. We introduce a novel class of valuation structures termed "structured submodular" valuations, which are both submodular and admit efficient computation for maximizing individual utility under such conditions. For this subset of structured submodular valuations, we demonstrate that the serial dictatorship mechanism guarantees a constant fraction of the optimal social utility. Additionally, we generalize these findings to broader valuation types, including those submodular with respect to specific agents and those submodular with respect to the entire valuation vector. Finally, we address a specific interest in bi-valent games—a two-player subcase of multi-player interaction—and prove a near-linear time approximation algorithm achieving a tight 2-approximation for optimizing social utility within bi-valent structured submodular games.

Our supplements include proofs for large-sample characteristics of the estimators discussed, various additional results with graphical illustrations, and table-based observations. This paper introduces several variations of Leibniz rules specifically formulated for Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative operators. It establishes the fundamental rules of multiplication, division, and chaining—known respectively as the product, quotient, and chain rules—applied to both types of operators. A particular focus is placed on the product rule, where three distinct formulations are proven: the classical version, an inverted variant, and a mid-type intermediate formulation. Additionally, these product rules are extended to apply individually to both integral and operator fractions. To support these theoretical developments, specific examples are provided to illustrate the applications of these newly formulated fractional calculus laws.

We introduce G4C (Goal-driven Guidance Generation for Game Playing in the Classroom), a new framework designed to create instructional commentary for role-playing games such as *Dungeons and Dragons*. This framework leverages the pedagogical tradition where educators enhance student development through purposeful complementaries to learners' choices within the game. G4C represents the first automatic system capable of constructing these educational narratives based on user inputs in RPGs. Our approach focuses on G4C meeting two essential criteria: (i) ensuring all user inputs lead to solvable game states via some sequence of actions, and (ii) guaranteeing such state transitions align with an intended story arc. To achieve this, we developed an automatic mechanism for generating RPG moves that both render states reachable and satisfy defined conditions reflecting desired commentaries. Furthermore, we created a new annotation protocol designed specifically for RPA (Role-Playing Assistant) to assign logical conditions to user inputs and target story milestones. Ultimately, we demonstrate through extensive testing on live sessions of *Dungeons and Dragons* that G4C can successfully generate both a functional response to user inputs and meaningful narrative text.

Recent advances in protein synthesis enable the assignment of specific knot types to individual proteins, creating a need for new analytical frameworks. This study introduces the use of knotoids—distinguished from knots by an open end representing a free chain terminus—to model and analyze both the topological and geometric attributes of proteins. We establish a theoretical basis for classifying knotoids through their knotoids-classes under topological equivalence and assess their geometric characteristics via the invariants derived from the free endpoint's movement in spatial models. We demonstrate that specific features of the protein structure dictate the range of motions available to this endpoint. Furthermore, we define a knotoid type based on the restricted movements of the free end within three-dimensional space and employ this concept to analyze the protein 5G4C41. This particular protein exhibits a full extension of the free chain end, allowing one knot type to accommodate various spatial configurations of the chain's terminal point.

A recent finding (arXiv:2007.07431v2) establishes an anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem, which demonstrates that imposing the canonical commutation relations on a compressed symmetry generator necessitates the violation of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. This discovery complicates the standard hypothesis of continuous symmetry breaking within quantum mechanics. Furthermore, it suggests that the compatibility of the canonical commutation relations must be reconsidered, given that they appear to conflict with fundamental principles of continuous symmetry breaking.

Recent research into data augmentation via generation of counterfactuals (GDAC) aims to provide training examples that facilitate learning by different paths, yet current approaches largely fail to produce data that is both realistic and faithful. We introduce GDAC as a framework designed to create data points that are not only genuine and feasible in practice but also follow the intended contrastive concept modifications. To achieve this, we apply word-level transformations within a large language model (LLM) context to derive corresponding prompt changes, an approach to which the model-specific decoder is then adapted for continuation. Our contributions significantly enhance a model's capacity for data-driven inference through two key areas: first, during pre-training, it improves the accuracy of natural language inference (NLIs) as models age; and second, after training, fine-tuning shows improved capacity for generalizing and producing more consistent output.

Remote epitaxy, where lattice-matched crystals form on substrates separated by barriers like sulfur monolayers or hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), has rarely been demonstrated for Heusler alloys. This study demonstrates the remote growth of Cobalt Titanate (Co2TiC) on graphene/H-BN/Si(111) substrates via magnetron sputtering of equimolar TiCo deposits onto the same Si(111)/h-BN/graphene/SO2 monolayer/SO2 configuration used previously for direct growth. Although the resulting Co2TiC shares the same crystallographic orientation as the underlying substrate, the epitaxial alignment occurs despite a 0.37% lattice mismatch between the substrate and the Co2TiC surface. Given that SO2 and h-BN are both epitaxial, we attribute the observed alignment to a mechanism where SO2 induces the formation of a moiré superlattice with the underlying substrate, which in turn facilitates the epitaxial nucleation of Co2TiC. Furthermore, introducing SO2 was found to suppress the typical epitaxial growth of Heusler phases, resulting instead in polycrystalline films. Collectively, these discoveries offer definitive proof of remote growth and establish SO2-assisted epitaxy as a viable strategy for engineering novel heterostructures of functional materials over existing stacks of tailored monolayers.

Conditional Generative Adverse Networks (cGANs) have demonstrated superior efficacy and versatility across a broad spectrum of generation tasks classified by their conditions. However, their application performance often fluctuates significantly based on how those conditions are formulated. We introduce Conditionally Generative Adverse Networks with Transform (cGANs-WT), an automated method designed to discover optimal condition transformations to boost model effectiveness. Our approach requires no prior assumptions regarding the condition's characteristics or assumptions about its transformation type. We evaluate our method on nine diverse conditions derived from four distinct datasets. The results indicate that automatic transformation discovery using our approach substantially outperforms both hand-crafted transformation strategies and the untransformed baseline.

The provenance of GeV gamma-rays originating from radio galaxies remains obscure, given that accretion efficiency appears too minimal to generate such emissions. We demonstrate, utilizing the UHURAGUM 2 catalog of radio sources detected by Fermi-LAT, that these findings provide robust constraints on the maximum energy of electrons and protons within CTA-10 and other similar radio galaxies. Importantly, the GeV cutoff observed in the spectrum of CTA-10 cannot stem from electron synchrotron processes peaking in the soft X-ray band; rather, it must result from the spilling of the proton threshold for hadronic interactions. The data from CTA-10 necessitates that the same physical mechanism responsible for the GeV cutoff extends deeper into the N49 remnant, a requirement inconsistent with current models of that supernova remnant. Regarding other objects in the UHURAGUM catalog, the analysis indicates that their entire observed GeV emission likely arises from the propagation of cosmic rays within the surrounding interstellar medium.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a critical point-of-care technique for identifying cardiac diseases early. Although deep-learning approaches have recently advanced the automated analysis of heart-sounds, these models often require extensive computational resources, hindering their integration into mobile medical systems. To address this limitation, we introduce VaDDy, a real-time deep-learning framework for automatic heart disease detection. VaDDy utilizes efficient architecture components and trains via self-supervised learning to ensure minimal, high-quality annotations are sufficient. Furthermore, our method incorporates a continuous learning strategy to facilitate updates without the need for retraining. Validation against the PhysioNet heart-sounds dataset demonstrated that VaDDy achieves an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.90333, confirming its potential for deployment on mobile devices for reliable heart-disease diagnosis.

The rapid advancement of algorithms and connectivity has made wearable health technology essential for personalizing user data. However, two major hurdles remain: ensuring the secure transmission of data and establishing robust personalization models. Addressing these hurdles is particularly critical for healthcare applications, where integrating model updates and user data across non-IID (independent and identically distributed) distributed nodes faces significant privacy risks due to aggregation bottlenecks and centralization. Drawing on federated learning principles, we introduce a novel framework designed to simultaneously personalize and train models directly on a device's cloud server. Our approach employs a dual-kernel convolutional neural network that adapts continuously to individual user characteristics while maintaining data privacy. To achieve this, we develop two distinct strategies for model updates: a recursive algorithm for wearable nodes and a data sampling technique for hospital nodes. Both methods facilitate private, distributed, and iterative training. Extensive experiments validate the framework's effectiveness, demonstrating superior accuracy in node personalization compared to state-of-the-art federated learning approaches.

This study examines various methods of portfolio optimization that incorporate higher moments like kurtosis (or skewness) alongside return and risk. Our work applies, adapts, and compares four specific approaches: the Black-Light model, the robust optimization framework by Soyster, the robust optimization technique with only hedging returns developed by Ben-Tal et. al., and the optimization framework proposed for maximum utility by our department. We present new derivations, provide important corrections, and introduce an additional category of problem formulation involving hierarchical optimization. Furthermore, we focus particularly on problem (iv), detailing its specific characteristics. Specifically, we detail its formulation as a fourth-order problem in non-linear optimization, exploring the nature of the resulting feasible region and the contour maps of the objective function. To complete the investigation, we conduct a computational study comparing these techniques based on the statistical properties and the frequency distributions (also known as the Pareto curves) associated with different numbers of shares.

Recruiting within large organizations typically involves extensive interview schedules that require careful planning and adaptability to various constraints, including the interviewer's limited availability, the need to minimize travel, and deadlines for completing the process. This paper introduces a system designed to generate robust recruitment interview agendas by addressing these factors. Our approach begins with a suitable formulation of the agenda generation task and introduces the introduction of a new metric to evaluate a schedule's quality: its resilience. This metric assesses how well an interview plan withstands changes in input data, specifically unavailability and shifts in interview durations. Furthermore, we present two distinct algorithms designed to create resilient interview agendas. Our experimental results indicate that more resilient schedules effectively accommodate disruptions, such as unexpected schedule conflicts, with only a marginal decline in solution quality. Additionally, these results demonstrate the importance of incorporating duration variations and different types of unavailability into the generation process itself.

We introduce the first DNA-storage architecture capable of supporting general data structures, specifically enabling indexed updates and dynamic data management. While previous DNA storage systems were restricted to garbage-collected flash storage or static data, our approach defines a logical B-tree structure. We handle all operations—synthesis, hybridization, and amplification—using standard biochemical protocols to manipulate nodes and pointers within this logical tree. Our method supports practical indexing by employing a 2D DNA storage lattice (a DNA B-tree) to manage the one-dimensional bitvector typically required for indexing. Subtrees and vector blocks are stored directly as oligonucleotides or short sequences. Furthermore, we developed an automated synthesis pipeline for this architecture and have physically built and tested a prototype system. Our lab results demonstrate a capacity for 36.6 GB per milliliter, a retrieval accuracy exceeding 99.9%, and operations taking under 1.5 days for 1TB datasets, including updates.

Accurately and reliably predicting river flow velocities is critical for various applications, including flood forecasting and the assessment of aquatic health. While traditional numerical solvers for the Navier-Stokes equations remain a primary tool for analyzing these shallow water flows, there is growing interest in developing machine learning (ML) alternatives. This study introduces a novel, data-driven approach to an unsteady shallow water flow problem, which represents the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations integrated over depth to form a set of two-dimensional inviscid relations. Specifically, we employ Longuet-Higgins and Dean's (1964) second-order theory, which offers an excellent description of linear, laminar flow within the boundary layer. Our work utilizes Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to create a simplified, rapid model for unsteady flow velocity that requires minimal input data. We conduct a detailed investigation into the model's performance, testing it against both simple analytical solutions and complex numerical simulations. By validating the method with an extended and challenging multi-variable case, we demonstrate that the proposed ML algorithm provides an effective and robust solution for predicting flow velocities.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging captures the full range of exposure levels within a single frame, significantly enhancing target detection and tracking in visual navigation systems. This article outlines a novel technique for conventional HDR image acquisition that merges multiple frames taken with different exposures. By employing a deep-learning framework, this method achieves instantaneous capture of a single-drawn HDR image with an arbitrary dynamic range, effectively avoiding software fusion issues like ghosting often seen in multi-frame approaches. Empirical results indicate that when configured for a dynamic range of 10.00 dB, this HDR-LSTM model outperforms standard low-dynamic systems in both detection performance and tracking accuracy.

Causal deep learning represents a significant and emerging subfield of machine learning focused on robust predictions and meaningful post-model analysis. Although substantial theoretical groundwork has been established for specific causal DL architectures, the broader theoretical landscape remains sparse. To address this, we introduce a novel framework grounded in the Structural Causal Model, designed to elucidate the behavioral properties of general deep learning structures while identifying reversible, high-level states within the network. We demonstrate that based on these identified states, one can derive precise theoretical bounds for prediction accuracy. Furthermore, by examining state transitions conditioned on these formal bounds, we establish corresponding causal effects with guaranteed accuracy. Key to this methodology is demonstrating that specific features occupy distinct regions in the network that facilitate effective separation. Ultimately, we view this framework as a foundational starting point for further theoretical advancements in causal deep learning.

This note introduces and analyzes a new class of maps known as oriented colored broken submersions. It represents the most fundamental class of maps complying with an h-principle (here referred to as b-principle); in two dimensions, it approximates oriented submersions notably by ensuring every oriented colored broken submersion from a 2-manifold to a closed, simply-connected target is concordant to a true submersion. Our proof technique relies heavily on the analysis of one-codimensional oriented burning submersions, from which an independent result—the oriented burning submersion b-principle in one case—is also derived.

This study presents a performance evaluation comparing two preconditioners intended for cardiac mechanics simulations solved via the finite element method and the Operator-Splitting Finite Element (OSFEL) scheme. The focus is on showing that the multigrid method (specifically two-level MG), which demonstrates excellent parallel performance on its own, can further enhance the Two-Level Multigrid (TMG) method's scalability. The analysis examines both field and time data during solution processes, covering memory consumption, floating-point operations, and communication metrics. Results are derived from simulations of left heart models on meshes containing approximately 300,000 elements, run on up to 1,024 cores using the HPCG benchmark suite.

Standard diffusive expansion is typified by a Gaussian distribution where the mean square displacement scales linearly against time, yet this standard behavior fails when correlations or heterogeneity arise. Consequently, this study analyzes the diffusion of fractional (long-time memory-corrupted) Brownian motion under varying concentrations of spatially diverse environments. The findings reveal that when Brownian motion operates within the presence of such diversity, the resulting distribution adheres formally to a Gompertz curve, effectively mirroring empirical demographic data for human populations over their entire lifespan. Consequently, the linear growth of mean square distance here signifies an inverse relationship: more heterogeneous societies exhibit lower rates of population dispersion. The paper concludes by offering biological interpretations linking these mathematical insights specifically to the context of viral propagation.

We examine the interplay of linear coupling, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity within pairs of optical resonators. This research demonstrates that such systems can produce a range of intricate behaviors, specifically including both Hopf and chaotic bifurcations. Our study focuses on two specific configurations: first, an untuned pair exhibiting a symmetry-breaking chaotic attractor where the attractor displays varying levels of symmetry, directly influenced by the degree of resonance mismatch; and second, an optimally tuned pair that is essentially symmetric, yet exhibits an attractive set that is not symmetric with respect to transmission and reflection modes. These observations are supported by numerical simulations, analytical derivations, and experimental prototypes operating in the near-infrared spectrum. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of a "symmetry-chaotic" index designed to quantify these atypical asymmetric characteristics of the attractor.

This study introduces a deep learning framework that utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to recover high-resolution turbulent velocity fields from very low-resolution data across various Reynolds numbers. The Multiscale Enhanced Super-Resolution GAN (MS-ESRGAN) serves as the model, taking $16\times$ downsampled datasets as input to generate fields at the original resolution with a $\times$ up factor of . Specifically, we address turbulent flows characterized by geometric complexity, including flow past a sphere, within a cubical enclosure with and without baffles, and around an automotive model. Success is measured by comparing generated fields against proper orthogonal decomposition (PROPO) coefficients and streamwise vorticity variations at different cross-sections of the test domains for each scenario. The results indicate that the model effectively reconstructs fields with $ up factor of 16, preserving key features such as flow separation points and reattachment points with a physical plausibility that exceeds standard super-resolution methods employing mean absolute error (MAE) or mean squared error (MSE) loss functions.

Although significant advancements have been made in applying reinforcement learning to robotics, gaming, and other domains, substantial challenges persist when addressing open-world issues. These models frequently generalize poorly to new environments or unencountered tasks, demanding extensive manual rule-setting or the deployment of closed systems. Recognizing that the primary difficulty for agents lies in navigating and understanding complex environments, we present WorldGen—a novel framework enabling an agent to automatically discover, comprehend, and generalize to new or unseen settings within a game world while simultaneously identifying and comprehending games it has never played before. WorldGen integrates four key components: a passive data collection system for comprehensive exploration, a continuous natural language environment description service, a self-supervised captioning task to encourage structure in those descriptions, and a dedicated learning environment constructed from this organized textual data. Test results demonstrate that agents trained via this method can successfully execute zero-shot generalization on various tasks, including those introduced after their initial training.

Process discovery algorithms aim to create process models directly from event logs, serving as a key method for understanding complex business operations. These emerging technologies complement other analytics approaches to extract insights from data. Nevertheless, the computational difficulty of these discovery tasks has received limited attention. This paper examines the computational complexity of various discovery problems, demonstrating that decision variants of these tasks are generally NP-complete and optimization versions are often strongly NP-hard. We also introduce specific polynomial-time solvable cases and establish NP-completeness for several problem variants that were previously unresolved. Finally, we offer a detailed analysis of these findings, discussing their implications in depth.

We have examined the connection between formation rates of bulges and their surrounding disks by analyzing a subset of 1389 EAGLE simulation galaxies. For each mock galaxy, we measured individual bulge and disk formation rates using independent semi-analytic techniques applied to substructure components identified through the N-body simulations' global $de Vaucouleurs$ and exponential surface brightness profiles, respectively. By correlating these bulge formation indicators with the star formation rates specific to the bulges themselves, we confirmed previously observed trends within the simulated data. Furthermore, this analysis reveals a complementary trend: the stellar mass fraction residing in bulges increases with the bulge-specific formation indicator. These findings collectively indicate that bulges tend to form in the most massive galaxies where formation occurs preferentially within the bulge region rather than the disk region, yet they do not provide insights into the internal star formation mechanisms specific to bulge structures alone. Additionally, our results demonstrate a strong correlation between the stellar mass formation functions for bulges and disk structures, as well as their respective scatter values, when utilizing characteristic substructure parameters such as the Sersic index and scale length. Consequently, current findings suggest that current-generation substructure decomposition methods, which rely on these fundamental indices derived from surface brightness profiles, are insufficient for explaining bulge formation mechanisms within the context of the massive galaxies modeled by the EAGLE project.

This research investigates cross-lingual sentiment analysis for Croatian news through semi-supervised and fully unsupervised methods. The study evaluates the following techniques: (i) transfer learning from English news sentiment tasks, (ii) supervision from unlabelled Croatian data paired with minimal English labeled data, (iii) supervision using exclusively unlabelled Croatian data, and (vi) supervision with unlabelled multilingual data. The paper compares the performance outcomes of these approaches, assessing their efficacy in the specific domain of Croatian sentiment classification.

Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) is increasingly vital for advanced human-centric object interaction analysis. Nevertheless, current models frequently yield a high false-positive rate, largely because the procedure for generating bounding boxes for object detectors is flawed. When a detector identifies an object pair, its cropping module typically selects two individual boxes, connecting them only via their closest edges. However, when objects are partially occluded, this simple connection method may erroneously link disjoint parts of the same entity or distinct groups, ultimately causing the model to predict spurious visual relations. Addressing this challenge, we present VOCAT, an approach to refine bounding box connections specifically for VRD. Uniquely, VOCAT refines these connections directly within the training pipeline of VRD frameworks. We devised a policy for learning an optimal connection between two boxes by integrating a graph-based learning algorithm with the training process of deep neural networks. Furthermore, a dedicated convolutional network was trained to predict the most likely connection path between object pairs. Because this approach ensures well-structured input coordinates for detectors, it lowers false positives by preventing them at the detection phase. Most notably, VOCAT achieved state-of-the-art performance across all metrics in the standard benchmarks for VRD.

We utilize high-resolution integral field data from the DEEPLESS survey covering 112 massive, locally selected galaxies to examine the mechanics behind reduced star formation in those featuring curved or asymmetric stellar disks. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between reduced specific star formation rates (sSFR) and increased stellar flaring, alongside findings that rule out both older stellar populations and reduced gas fractions in galaxies with more curved disks as primary causes for diminished star formation activity. We observe reduced gas kinematic tension and specific angular momentum in these systems, even after normalizing discrepancies due to gravitational effects from disk curvature or warping. Furthermore, we note a lack of connection between reduced star formation and external quenching mechanisms such as ram pressure stripping or group interactions. Collectively, these results point toward an intrinsic mechanism responsible for curbing star formation in galaxies with curved or asymmetric disks; however, current data remain insufficient to confirm if this occurs due lower specific angular momentum or kinematic stability. This phenomenon likely accounts for a substantial portion of the intrinsic quenching seen in most massive galaxies.

Our search for Solar Neutron Decay Protons (SNDP) at the TIGRESS medium-stopping gamma-ray spectrometer involved analyzing data collected between 2016 and 2019 during solar flares. These events were identified via their characteristic double escape peak in the 9.1 Mev region, resulting from the annihilation of positrons generated when neutrons decay into protons and neutrons near the Sun's surface. Although detected indirectly through this annihilation signature, the direct observation of neutrons escaping the Sun remains an elusive goal; historically, Solar Neutrons have only been observed near the Earth or by satellites, precluding direct detection at their origin. To account for potential undercounting, we developed a simulation incorporating geometric acceptance, efficiency, and background constraints to estimate the required flux excess—a tenfold increase over standard solar activity—necessary for observable events. Despite analyzing data from major flares, most facilitated by the DSN and GEMS networks, including the significant G1 and G2 events, we were unable to confirm the presence of SNDP. Consequently, based on our null result, we establish an upper limit for these proton signals corresponding to less than half the intensity previously required in similar experiments.

The theoretical modeling of stellar evolution, particularly for low-luminosity giant stars where luminosity originates from deep within the star rather than the surface, often encounters difficulties in accurately representing angular momentum transport. This study employs the MECADE code to simulate a 1D giant evolution track for a 1.2 solar mass star on a log t scale from -3 through -1. Our findings indicate that discontinuities in specific angular momentum arise at the core-envelope boundary due to complex magnetic interactions and shear stresses. Additionally, we analyzed the impact of internal magnetic fields on field generation mechanisms such as the Tayler-Spruit dynamo, observing field strengths of approximately 100 Gauss near the envelope-core interface and 10-100 Gauss within the envelope. Our results demonstrate that Core-envelope interactions (CEnI) effectively reproduce the core-envelope mismatch phenomenon known as the Core Helioseismic Effect (CORE), which manifests as a sudden drop in giant surface rotation following ignition. This occurs because the code forces specific angular momentum discontinuity upon crossing the giant branch, enabling surfaces to reach lower rotation rates while the rapidly spinning cores remain unaltered. Our findings also align with the concept of a Central Condensation of Rotation (CCR), predicting surface rotations of 0.5 to 1.0 times the critical limit for the turn-off main sequence, matching recent empirical data. Our results also support the Central CCR theory, predicting surface rotations of 0.5 to 1.

Rapidly circulating through social media, fake news poses a significant threat to the digital landscape, with deepfake technologies accelerating their dissemination. Consequently, identifying such content regarding emerging events has become a primary focus for researchers. However, our analysis reveals that current detection frameworks are hindered by the necessity for extensive, curated datasets and specialized training frameworks tailored to specific news topics. These methods struggle to generalize when encountering different subjects. Addressing this gap, we introduce Framework for Real-Fake Detection for Real-Time (FoDaDa)—a framework designed for real-time identification of fake coverage of emerging incidents. FoDaDa leverages social media activity from the first day of an event's emergence, requiring no prior training on large, curated collections. Furthermore, it establishes a unified framework connecting various reporting sources, arguing that the sequential order in which information appears across these sources provides crucial clues to authenticity. Our experiments on real-world data confirm that Fake verification systems using FoDaDa achieve an F1 score exceeding 0.89.

Quantum tunneling and Coulomb interactions are fundamental physical phenomena that appear across a vast array of scientific and engineering fields. Although prior research using silicon's phosphorus dopants demonstrated the ability to prepare and measure their interaction energy, those studies lacked the capacity to directly image its spatial distribution. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a method to measure the through-space interaction between individual dopants by observing nuclear spins. This approach relies on using silicon-29 host atoms as spin sensors for a neighboring doped phosphorus atom. We calibrated the through-space interaction with such precision that we were able to map its through-plane variance. The ultimate precision of the interaction energy is predominantly governed by how uniformly the dopant lies within the silicon plane; therefore, achieving better vertical positioning control will further enhance measurement accuracy. Employing phosphorus dopants as qubits, we detail how to utilize these systems to actively compensate for their mutual interaction energy.

Complex systems made up of interconnected elements can be handled effectively as regression problems by framing them within the framework of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). This approach is particularly useful for systems like traffic networks or electricity grids, where the behavior of individual nodes depends on their interactions. In fields such as finance and weather forecasting, although system states are often high-dimensional and sparse, it turns out that the underlying dynamics remain the same. Even in these vast state spaces, using an "invariant" approach allows us to treat them as manageable graph structures where relationships between nodes are consistent. By applying this logic, we can apply the learned patterns from a small subset of states to predict outcomes across the entire spectrum. This generalization capability is crucial when dealing large numbers of unverified nodes or limited data points, such as new financial assets or new weather conditions. Ultimately, these findings indicate that for certain classes of dynamical systems, analyzing node interactions through GNNs provides a powerful method for both understanding and prediction.

Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a new minimally invasive technique for ablating intracranial mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE) lesions, such as low-grade gliomas, though current segmentation methods for MRI data supporting LITT planning and evaluation lack the necessary accuracy. This study introduces U-Net-based deep learning models enhanced with multi-scale feature fusion and attention mechanisms to accurately retrieve enhanced MRI components specifically for LITT treatment planning. Furthermore, another developed model automatically characterizes these components to label pixels as "treated," "ablated," or "healthy" within the MRI scans. Utilating enhanced MRI data augmentation and semi-supervised learning strategies on annotated MRI from the RATS consortium, the enhanced convolutional networks were evaluated for robustness and accuracy. The proposed approach achieved a mean surface distance (MSD) of 0.83 $\pm$ 0.19 mm between automatically generated contours and expert annotations in the "treated" region of interest, effectively facilitating contouring in the "ablated" region of interest with similar performance metrics. These outcomes indicate that the proposed method's capability in accurately characterizing post-LITT MRI scans and supports clinical utility in analyzing the impact of the procedure on low- grade intracranial epilepsy.

Model selection or sparse modeling for categorical variables remains challenging, even with a limited number of features. Standard approaches typically involve converting categorical variables into binary indicators and applying selection methods directly to this expanded high-dimensional vector; however, this results in uninterpretable outcomes due to constraints ignored during the process. Alternatively, model fitting could theoretically occur separately for each subgroup (level) of every variable; in practice, however, this is often infeasible because such a strategy requires substantially more data or assumes homogeneous structure across the entire model. We introduce a new algorithm designed to impose sparsity directly within the space of these binary components. This method enables the identification or formulation of multiple hierarchical patterns among all other types of variable group sparsity. Our techniques demonstrate robust performance through both synthetic experiments and analysis of real datasets.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable natural language comprehension and generation capabilities, equipping them with structured knowledge from Knowledge Graphs (KGs) often proves more effective and efficient than furnishing them with equivalent KG sentences via methods like Instruction Tuning. To address this, we introduce GraphFever, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the Fearless Evolution (Fe2) framework. Our evaluations demonstrate that Fe2 achieves a significant 5.3 Fe2 score improvement over using standard KG statements, with these results scaling further across diverse datasets and additional real-world applications. We also offer in-depth analyses exploring the Fe2 phenomenon, its impact on evaluation metrics, and the specific contributions of different KG structural elements. The Fe2 framework's source code and weights are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Fe2-KG/GraphFever.

Spatial anti-aliasing is critical for both the visual quality and rendering performance of line joins where road segments intersect on vector maps. Given OpenGL's limitations, a standard approach involves using quads to approximate circular joins; however, this often results in a visually unappearing square shape. This study presents two proposed methods for anti-aliased line connections: one employing quadrantic arcs and the other utilizing sub-divided arcs. The proposed solutions were evaluated against the conventional quad method through comparative analysis of rendering throughput and memory usage. Additionally, a novel algorithm for subdividing arcs was developed to ensure high-performance rendering across various screen resolutions without producing visual artifacts, ultimately demonstrating clear superiority over the traditional quad technique in this research.

Recent years have seen a growing interest in multi-fluid models, a framework that applies faradaic hydrodynamics to atmospheric research. Although weather and climate models currently rely on convection parameterizations, proponents argue that embracing multi-fluid hydrodynamics could substantially enhance them. The core innovation of these models is their ability to separate stratified fluids into distinct, faradaic interfaces between multiple interacting fluids. In the context of the atmosphere, the lower boundary represents the ground, while the upper boundary is marked by convection elements treated as individual fluids with their own interfaces. Because the pressure and temperature remain continuous and well-mixed within each convective element, these local units can accurately simulate turbulent mixing. Furthermore, since interface dynamics are governed by well-established mathematical laws, they provide a robust mechanism for representing convective processes. While previous studies have used this approach in two dimensions, extending the model to three dimensions is essential for effectively simulating real-world atmospheric conditions. This study therefore presents the first three-dimensional multi-fluid hydrodynamic model, detailing the numerical techniques employed to manage the interface dynamics inherent in this system.

We examine three independent Jaynes-Cummings systems involving atom pairs where correlations exist between some atoms while the third remains initially uncorrelated. Our analysis reveals a key condition: achieving true multipartite entanglement among the three uncorrelated atoms requires genuinely correlated (non-separable) initial states. By introducing a measure of both atomic and field multipartite entanglement, we quantify these properties across various initial scenarios. Specifically, we investigate the transition from initial atomic entanglement to final cavity entanglement. Our findings demonstrate that while the degree of multipartite entanglement transferred to the fields varies depending on the initial atomic state correlations, the capacity to generate such entanglement in the fields is universal; specifically, any initial atomic state that is itself multipartite entangled will inevitably produce multipartite entangled states within the cavity fields.

Emotional monitoring on platforms like Twitter through sentiment analysis serves companies, organizations, and researchers by offering insights into the sentiments of users. However, the reliance on deep neural networks in this process often results in high computational costs. To address this, the proposed approach introduces a novel framework termed Emotion-Aware BERT (EaBERT), designed to maintain high performance while ensuring cost-effective operations. The core innovation of this method involves utilizing a multi-level fusion strategy for embeddings and implementing a dynamic filter mechanism to selectively train only those layers influenced by input data. The effectiveness of the proposed technique was evaluated across two distinct datasets comprising English tweets. The outcomes demonstrate that the proposed approach not only matches state-of-the-art performance standards but also exhibits significant reductions in both computational complexity and training time compared to existing methods.

This study investigates the first-order deconfiment phase transition in the $d$-dimensional ($d>3$) Einstein--Maxwell--Dilaton--Axion (EMDA) black hole within its extreme regime. Using geometric criteria, the thermodynamic nature of these serial EMDA transitions is evaluated via the shadow radius ($r_s$) and shadow temperature ($T_s$). The findings reveal that both the Shannon entropy ($S_{Sh}$) and specific heat ($C$) exhibit clear singularities exactly when the radial and thermal profiles reach a similar point. Such behavior confirms that analyzing shadow radii and their corresponding Shannon entropies offers a viable approach for understanding the EMDA series of alternatives.

Reconstructing quantum states in continuous-variable systems like the radiation field faces obstacles primarily stemming from the substantial dimensionality of the associated Hilbert space. Various reconstruction techniques exist, yet they often encounter practical barriers. Conversely, methods based on classical and Wigner functions derived from O'Gorman et al.'s formula require a state of light with known classical probability distribution. This study employs state-light interactions to map out the complete Wigner function using an optical table setup. Our approach utilizes the direct measurement and recording of optical tomograms alongside the application of the inverse of O'Gorman's formula. By performing this measurement under diverse parameters—specifically local oscillation amplitudes and detection efficiencies—we demonstrate through both simulation and real experiments the effective reconstruction of various states of light.

360-degree video streaming delivers immersive user experiences across online platforms. Specifically, virtual tourism leverages this technology to allow remote users to explore real-world landmarks by looking around in an unlimited landscape. However, the ability to download these high-resolution, large-scale videos quickly and efficiently remains a significant challenge. Current approaches typically rely on a global delivery strategy that does not account for the gazing behavior of individual viewers. Our proposed solution integrates gaze-directed streaming tailored for immersive virtual reality (VR) touring. This approach utilizes virtual guides to approximate viewer gaze directions, enabling a content prioritization algorithm that adaptively selects which video blocks to enhance or degrade based on this insight. We evaluated the system using two distinct datasets: a live dataset capturing actual user gaze data from VR tourists visiting the Forbidden City in Beijing, and a simulated dataset generating synthetic gaze patterns. The study also compares our method against an existing gaze-adaptive baseline. The results, particularly regarding viewable resolution from the perspective of users, demonstrate the method's effectiveness and superiority over current standards.

Nanometer-thick rare-earth-transition metal (RE-TM) alloys, characterized by their naturally formed spontaneous magnetic domains and ultrafast dynamics, present an appealing yet challenging platform for developing magnetophotonic nanostructures when combined with plasmonic antenna arrays. We demonstrate the creation of such hybrid structures by patterning Au/TbCo films onto lithographically defined TiO2 plasmonic nanoantenna arrays. The magnetic state of the TbCo layer was precisely controlled by adjusting film thickness, enabling the system to switch between single- and multi-domain configurations. These states produce distinct, size-dependent scattering patterns when interacting with the TiO2 antennas under both transmission and reflection modes of operation. These results indicate that the proposed fabrication technique yields hybrid magnetoplasmonic nanostructures capable of generating either multi-directional or radially symmetric cone diffraction patterns, depending on whether the RE-TM component is in a single or multi-domain magnetic state.

Knowledge distillation serves as a proven strategy for expediting deep neural networks, where a compact "student" model learns from a larger "teacher" network. Although effective, the process often suffers from reduced performance due to the simplified representations provided by the teacher. To address this, we propose introducing multiple expert models rather than relying on a single teacher, arguing that this diverse ensemble is capable of representing student behaviors more accurately. However, the increased complexity of these expert combinations poses computational challenges. Our solution employs a shared sparsity structure within the student architecture, allowing it to express the combined dynamics of the experts through the sparse activation of specific network pathways. Extensive testing on standard image classification benchmarks demonstrates that this simultaneous activation and sharing (SAS) framework with structured pruning not only reduces the student's footprint but also enhances performance compared both to traditional knowledge distillation methods and untrained models of equivalent size when applied to the ResNet-50 architecture using the ImageNet dataset.

Constructing the submodule lattice $M$ for an arbitrary module $N$ is generally unfeasible. This paper introduces an algorithm that builds the lattice submodules $\mathcal L(N)$ for any module $N$ over a non-commutative NOIR ring $R$. The approach relies on identifying a collection of join-irreducible submodules within a given generating set for the lattice. Specifically, the proposed method computes these irreducible components using only a standard generator list for $L(N)$ and the membership testing procedure associated with a specific primality test.

Imitation learning primarily enhances reinforcement learning efficiency by utilizing expert demonstrations. However, obtaining such demonstrations is often prohibitive or unfeasible in real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new framework dubbed Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), designed to harness an agent's past high-quality interactions independent of external experts functions as it explores an environment it also takes advantage of peer agents past experiences. Both agents are engaged experience sharing. A key innovation of CoIL lies in how it refinements the process by which agents learn from one another; specifically, it calculates dynamic importance weights for contributed experiences based on how recently they were obtained and how accurate they are. This ensures that superior actions are more effectively extracted from historical action–reward pairs. Our series of experiments, including a real-world application, validates the framework, illustrating not only the effectiveness of Co-IM but also demonstrating how it ensures safety while agents exchange insights.

This paper proposes a new metric function for use with Polarization-Adjusted Convolutional (PAC) codes. The authors demonstrate that their function effectively enhances the error-correction capabilities of PAC codes under maximum-likelihood decoding, even in the presence of non-Gaussian channel non-linearities like inter-symbol interference. Additionally, the study introduces a non-linear decision feedback mechanism to further boost performance with non-linear channels. It is shown via simulation that, when integrated, these two contributions— the new metric function and decision feedback—enable PAC codes to achieve nearly the same error rates as convolutional codes decoded via turbo methods, despite utilizing sub-optimal (MAP) decoding. Although applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) after Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a common approach to improve Neural Machine Translation (NMT), recent studies suggest these improvements stem largely from smaller effective batch sizes rather than the reward signal itself. This paper proposes utilizing RL with an unchanged batch size after MLE pre-training to facilitate vocabulary reduction in NMT. To achieve this, we introduce a modified reward function that lowers values for translations involving rare words and employs active learning strategies to rapidly decrease the candidate generation lexicon. Experiments conducted on the WMT 2014 En-Gt and En-Fr datasets demonstrate successful reductions in vocabulary规模 while maintaining strong translation performance across both datasets. Additionally, scale-up tests on a crosslingual zero-training setup for En-Ss-Yost performed equally well compared to other approaches, achieving a better balance between output quality and efficiency.

The time-periodic dynamics of open quantum systems attract considerable interest due to their ability to reach a unique, dynamic balance characterized by continuous flow, distinguishing them from an isolated thermal steady state. This specific experimental work investigates the effects of periodic and discrete time driving on a single photon interacting with its environment. We present a robust theoretical modeling approach that accurately captures these phenomena, validating it through both numerical experiments and analytical calculations. A key outcome reveals a remarkable robustness against flow, where despite varying drive frequencies and photon loss rates, the system exhibits quasi-energy transitions changing only periodically with a frequency of half the drive, while maintaining identical characteristics across different drive regimes.

Although current SER models achieve strong outcomes on benchmark datasets, their application to real-world live data often results in decreased performance. This decline is primarily due to domain mismatches, which necessitates domain adaptation (DA) strategies. This paper introduces a universal framework designed to elevate existing base models across various scenarios. We evaluate the approach on two distinct setups: (1) new live data containing speaker diversity and noise, achieved by first aligning the base speaker and signal distributions via an adversarial speaker/channel alignment (AAA) module, and (2) various external datasets characterized by different emotions, accessed using an auxiliary classifier trained specifically for domain adaptation on those external sources. Consequently, the proposed methodology successfully boosts the results of multiple state-of-the-art (SOTA) SER approaches in live conditions and on external datasets.

Chances for upward mobility through college education, functioning as an intermediate variable, are extensively studied; yet, most research utilizes only the characteristics of young adults as their higher education attainment. This study employs data from the German Socological Panel to incorporate information about 17-year-old university students, accessible via official university records, into this framework using a sub-sample of SP children currently attending university. Our analysis demonstrates that including this university student data substantially elevates the predictive accuracy of the intergenerational transmission model among Germans.

In 2015, the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel luminosity scanning technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were conducted during physics runs at both 3.5 TeV and 6.5 TeV using full-intensity beam packages. This paper details the configuration, execution, and analysis of these scans based on data acquired from the ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and CBM experiments. The study also describes the application of machine-learning algorithms designed to optimize beam position during the scan process. Relying on precisions exceeding 1% for single-bunch luminosity measurements at all energy levels, the methods presented refine single-bunch luminosity determinations with sufficient accuracy to calibrate absolute luminosity scans based on total recorded counts.

This study addresses a distributed optimization challenge in multi-agent systems where a subset of nodes behave maliciously. Specifically, these adversaries attempt to drive the network off the optimal trajectory by corrupting data transmitted to their neighbors and imposing high bandwidth costs through excessive communication. Accordingly, we introduce a quantized, distributed gradient-based algorithm designed for benign agents. This section establishes the convergence of the proposed method to a vicinity of the global optimal solution, analyzing success under various bandwidth constraints and adversarial conditions. Finally, we present simulation results to validate the theory and demonstrate how the new approach outperforms existing methods in both reduced communication costs and faster convergence rates.

Detecting fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), often called anisotropies, is among the most challenging frontiers in cosmology. To study them effectively, next-generation instruments must operate at the extreme sensitivity limits allowed by instrumental noise and the vast, sparse, non-repeating scan patterns of the celestial sphere. This paper outlines our approach to reconstructing the CMB temperature anisotropy field and estimating their statistical properties using a non-linear non-uniform optimal estimation method implemented within a non-Markovian framework. This technique is designed around a forward physical and radiometric simulation of a specific non-uniform full-Sky microwave non-imaging array: the large non-uniform non-repeating non-imaging Atacama cosmology telescope (ACT). Preliminary results from a synthetic complete mock observation run utilizing this observation strategy and processing framework are also provided.

Word reordering represents a language generation challenge where models must arrange unordered inputs into coherent text using ordered output, based primarily on existing research employing standard models or neural networks. Despite this history, researchers have not yet investigated the benefits of large, word-oriented language models or proposed reasons why pre-trained ones succeed in these scenarios. In this work, we analyze why BART, a model trained on words, effectively handles sorting issues despite its lack of higher-level features like intent or entities. We propose three potential reasons for this performance: first, syntactic corrections inherent to pre-training; second, local ordering patterns learned during that phase; and and third, distributional word order cues embedded within the training data specifically tailored to these tasks and verified through attention mechanisms and ablation tests. Lastly, we test if adding explicit order information improves performance on the reversal task but find that the gains are limited.

The rapid advancement of deepfake technologies, which enable the realistic synthesis of videos and audio, has created an urgent need for effective detection frameworks. Although existing methods often concentrate solely on spatial data or ignore temporal and frequency domain insights, this research proposes a novel cross-domain framework for deepfake identification. This system integrates a convolutional neural network (NN) for frame-level analysis with a Neural Network for inter-NN interactions to identify synthetic content in videos and the resulting artifacts. Experiments conducted on the Forensics 20k dataset demonstrate that this hybrid approach significantly enhances individual NN performance, establishing it as a superior standalone detector. Additionally, extending the individual model yielded a 11.11% increase in accuracy, solidifying the effectiveness of the proposed model.

Community detection represents the most effective clustering strategy for systems that evolve over time. However, standard methods for identifying communities often require extensive mathematical frameworks and are too slow for large, extensive datasets. Furthermore, existing approaches lack the ability to handle both massive scales and maintain minimal latency. To solve these issues, we have engineered \texttt{DyNiClust}, a system designed to detect communities in dynamic, high-volume graphs quickly. It integrates two key innovations: (i) a streamlined, probabilistic version of the stochastic Blockmodel used to define communities, and (ii) two optimized data structures that enable efficient merging and splitting of community states. \texttt{DyNiClust} leverages Apache Flink to manage the transition and division logic between states. We evaluated the system using both synthetic and real-world datasets involving over one million nodes; our results demonstrate its feasibility and superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art solutions.

Implementing neural text generation models via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) presents significant challenges due to the non-differentiability of the full training loop, a limitation existing approaches address poorly. To effectively leverage the discriminative power of GANs without incurring current drawbacks, we introduce Cycle-Consistent Translation with Feature-level Guidance (CFG). This novel framework enhances translation without differentiable GANs by introducing two key innovations: first, a non-differentropic objective derived from cycle-consistency constraints; and second, a discriminative term that minimizes feature-level distances between generated and real samples according to pretrained parser and classifers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves over state-of-the-art techniques across multiple benchmarks in English and low-resource scenarios with Spanish and French.

The concept that life can migrate across planetary systems, known as interstellar panspermia, dates back decades but remains hard to validate through observation. To evaluate the chances of confirming this phenomenon, we established a mathematical framework accounting for factors such as the lifespan of resilient microbes in transit, the dispersion of stellar velocities, and the distribution of ejected material. Our results indicate that the statistical pair distribution of inhabited planetary systems can effectively detect interstellar transfer of life under the specific condition that ejecta move with sufficient divergence relative to stellar motions. By offering heuristic estimates and identifying observable constraints, we demonstrate that current and upcoming telescopes have the capacity to test the validity of interstellar panspermia.

A core focus of animal research involves modeling how space is utilized and how resources are selected. Although this field has significantly advanced through the application of statistical and machine learning techniques, there is typically little guidance on evaluating and comparing these specific models. This study introduces a unified framework designed to assess and compare wildlife location analysis models, utilizing spatial use and resource selection as either use-density or selection-ratio models. Relying on probabilistic back-transformation metrics, we evaluate whether new model predictions align with transformed averaged field observations, using calibration curves and associated root mean squared error scores. Beyond this novel assessment framework, we compare popular spatial use and selection models via standard selection for association, model selection, and multi-model inference. Specifically, we investigate the spatial use "focal points" (Kernels) and the "selection focal points" (logistic regression) models. Through simulated data encompassing various location and resource variables, we explore the selection focal points for association, model selection, and multi-model selection. Specifically, we investigate the spatial use "focal points" (Kernels) and the "selection focal points" (logistic regression) models.

Multilayer networks represent a valuable tool for modeling the diverse dynamics found in complex systems; however, most inferential methods currently rely on single-layer assumptions and often fail to capture the true dynamics or achieve high accuracy. This paper introduces data-driven approaches to estimate both directed and bipartite multilayer networks from time-series data, covering cases where node identities are known and where they remain unknown. Our methods, which utilize simple linear models, demonstrate performance that exceeds single-layer alternatives and effectively distinguish between multilayer and equivalent single-layer dynamics even when node labels are unidentified. Regarding labeled nodes, our inferential framework accurately identifies specific inter-layer connections, connection weights, and the topology of mappings between layers and network nodes—all based on time-series data alone.

abla \circ U \circ 
abla$, utilizing $U$ consisting of $m$-tuples related to the classical square root appearing in Fela's results.

Formal verification techniques have been broadened to accommodate extensive classes of programs, while also seeing the application of automation for identifying specific test cases during validation. However, these formal testing approaches often require extensive manual intervention, thereby restricting their utility for larger projects. To address this limitation, we introduce a technique for automatically generating execution tests. Our approach relies on an inferred representation derived from prior program runs to facilitate more effective alignment with standard dynamic testing frameworks.

We address the fundamental task of determining the majority element within a network of $n$ nodes, where some fraction may be compromised and behaving adversarially. In the synchronous, round-based model described here, our approach is effective even when up to $f = O(n^{.99})$ of the nodes are Byzantine. Notably, this is the first algorithm to achieve tolerance for super-extreme scaling of Byzantine failures (specific, $f = \omega(n^{1/2})$) that does not depend on knowing the exact count of bad nodes. Crucially run for only logarithmic time—precisely $O(\log n)$ rounds—it relies on the assumption that communication occurs even if nodes are faulty and messages are lost or altered during transmission. Our method is built upon an adaptation of the well-known, majority-determining Gosper's algorithm designed for limited crash failures, handling the complexities introduced by deception and unreliability from compromised sources.

Accurate traffic control depends on effectively estimating traffic states, particularly queue lengths. This research proposes an straightforward method for estimating conditional queue lengths at signalized intersections using trajectory data from probe vehicles. The method conditions location-based occupancy rates on the time-of-day and applies a negative binomial distribution to model the random variable of vehicles waiting in queues. A simple probe data collection scheme ensures these conditions can be met easily in practice. Although basic, the algorithm offers precise estimates of queue lengths without requiring deployment of complex or costly occupancy sensors.

Numerical relativity simulations involving non-trivial matter configurations require solving the ADM Hamiltonian and momentum constraints to determine initial data. Since these coupled, semi-discrete nonlinear equations lack an analytic solution for realistic scenarios, enforcing them is primarily used as a validity test in dynamical simulations. To address this, we apply a multigrid conjugate gradient method to solve the Hamiltonian constraint within a Pseudo-ISCO framework, utilizing a new orthogonal set of basis functions derived from our own construction. Our findings demonstrate a significant speedup in the convergence of constraint satisfaction compared to conventional techniques.

The resurgence in research regarding magnetic materials that display a significant anomalous Hall effect despite negligible magnetization stems from the desire to control and understand these phenomena. Antiferromagnetic materials are a key class within this field, where the robustness of the anomalous Hall effect has been linked to the geometric complexity of the Fermi surface and the non-trivial topology of the Berry curvature. However, quantitatively modeling the contribution of Berry curvature in antiferromagnetic systems remains challenging due to the intricate symmetry constraints of the lattice. This work presents the general formula for the 3D Berry curvature's 2C (two-cycle) classification within magnetic antiferromagnetic symmetry, streamlining the process for calculating Berry curvature-based Hall conductivity in these materials to determine their two-cycle character as a specific quantitative metric. The derived method is validated through the re-analysis of recent findings on the antiferromagnetic garnet HoMn$_6$O$_{14}$ and the film-forming antiferromagnetic perovskite MnIrO$_3$.

We present a generalization of Serre's conjecture applicable to GL_N for all N >= 2, utilizing Kummer theory, and this approach functions as follows: 1. the general N-case reduces effectively to the quadratic case (N=2); 2. the argument for the quadratic case proceeds directly in the infinite-level setting. For the exterior isoperimetric problem involving a compact obstacle, we establish a result at full resolution regarding minimizers within the high volume limit where $v \to \infty$. This result is derived by defining a novel concept known as Isaacsohn-Veronelli's number, demonstrating that in asymptotically large $v$ regimes, its value reaches the minimum possible over all shapes while also ensuring volume asymptotic behavior. Furthermore, in the case spherical obstacles, we establish that this number is minimum in the very large volume limit, and that all relevant shapes become planar in the infinite volume limit, with deviations vanishing as $v$ approaches infinity.

Fiber-reinforced composite materials are increasingly utilized in safety-critical applications, such as aircraft fuselages, necessitating effective methods for early failure identification. This paper details the application of carbon black (CB) and CB-coated steel fibers within a polymer matrix to establish a self-monitoring capability. Experimental results indicate that mechanical damage alters the material's surface-level electrical conductivity. By mapping surface resistivity using an electro-optical technique, researchers demonstrated the ability to identify and track various failure modes, including matrix cracks, delamination, and delamination repairs. Although this method currently detects surface-level phenomena, it serves as a viable proof of concept; subsequent research could extend these findings to assess internal structural integrity.

We challenge ourselves by examining how a public concern, often attributed to us, works: does the collective's insight rely on that of its members? Specifically, we investigate the link between public understanding and individual intelligence. Relying on a Facebook "like," which functions as an easy metric for opinion, we gathered data to test whether strong community views stem from intense individual views. Our findings indicate that such feedback is indeed relationship-dependent. We offer an original interpretation of this experience, finding value beyond simple preference aggregation.

Furthermore, fundamental topics in two-dimensional tensor analysis—specifically vector, dyadic, and higher-order tatic operations—are demonstrated through the lens of this novel framework."

We examine the characteristics of a muon and an exotic partner lemon, both neutral and accessing the dark sector through effective field theories. Our analysis reveals that imposing constraints on dark photon couplings to current leptons ensures two effects: significant propagation distances, which can reach meters, accompanied by prolonged lifetimes and distinct delayed signals. These findings apply universally whether the current leptons are identical or different. Additionally, we detail specific scenarios involving a dark photon coupled to non-access current leptons. In such cases, the combination of long lifetimes and substantial decay travel distances arises from suppressing both production and interaction within detectors while remaining unconstrained by existing bounds on oscillations between sectors.

Toda conformal field theory ( Toda CFT) serves as a natural extension of Liouville CFT, characterized by more intricate correlators. Within the Euclidean framework, these correlators emerge as solutions to a higher-order linear differential system, with the leading solution determined by a semi-classical WKB expansion involving a power of the coupling constant. In Toda CFT, this power corresponds to the rank of the underlying Lie algebra, while the sub-leading terms involve differential operators acting recursively. Specifically for Liouville CFT, this recursion was first outlined by Zamolodchikov and fully derived in the higher-genus context by Matone and Schiappa. We generalize this recursion within the matrix path integral setting of Toda CFT for all genera. This higher-dimensional extension not only encompasses the Liouville CFT hierarchy but also recovers the corresponding higher-genus Toda and classical Liouville chain models, with the latter additionally describing the Toda and hierarchies of integrable Hamiltonian systems.

We establish the biautomaticity of Coxeter groups, confirming an open problem posed by automatic groups advocates. Additionally, a criterion for characterizing bi-automatic Coxets based on their Fitting height is also provided.
